Le métier de prof doit (re)faire rêver BELGA. U n enseignant peut changer une vie, transmettre une passion, redonner confiance, repérer une fragilité… Il a aussi l’immense responsabilité d’outiller ses élèves pour en faire des citoyens éclairés. Ces derniers jours, dans Le Soir , les lettres à Monsieur Pol ou Madame Anne ont rappelé cette évidence : enseigner est l’un des plus précieux métiers de notre société. C’est utile de le souligner, un lundi de rentrée, alors que le fracas des réformes et des grèves nous l’avait presque fait oublier. Car quelque chose s’est grippé au royaume scolaire. Cette profession, si noble et si fondamentale, attire moins. De jeunes recrues abandonnent. Une hémorragie des vocations se dessine. Les témoignages recueillis ne trompent pas : fatigue, perte de sens, voire colère. « Lorsque les enseignants disent qu’ils se sentent méprisés, c’est une réalité, c’est un sentiment qu’on ne peut pas simplement balayer d’un revers de la main », reconnaît la ministre Valérie Glatigny (MR). Les raisons de ce malaise grandissant ? Des classes, d’abord, de plus en plus difficiles à tenir. L’attention des élèves, biberonnés au scroll, se disperse toujours plus vite. Des parents, ensuite, toujours plus présents. Parfois même envahissants ou prompts à contester une décision pédagogique, par recours officiel ou en s’épanchant sur les réseaux. Des réformes, surtout, qui s’enchaînent. Et que les enseignants encaissent avec le sentiment d’être vus politiquement comme une variable d’ajustement d’un budget à bout de souffle. D’une fracture avec l’opinion publique, enfin. Parce que les grèves se sont multipliées en ordre dispersé, sans toujours être comprises. Bref, un fossé se creuse sous nos yeux. Dangereusement. Bien sûr, la situation budgétaire de la Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles est catastrophique. Le métier d’enseignant doit, comme d’autres, évoluer. Des héritages du passé peuvent être questionnés. Mais il est urgent de faire embarquer à bord de ce train de réformes celles et ceux qui devront les porter : les profs. Jamais nous n’avons autant demandé à l’école. Mais rarement celles et ceux qui la font ont ressenti un tel mépris. L’urgence est de sortir de cette défiance et de redonner du désir et de la fierté à l’enseignement. Cela commence par une prise de conscience collective : être chaque jour face à une classe, c’est porter une part de l’avenir de dizaines de jeunes. Ça se prépare. Ça se vit. Et ça mérite le plus profond des respects – loin des caricatures de profs éternels vacanciers. Pour redorer ce blason, il faut aussi rendre aux enseignants de l’autonomie et une autorité pédagogique trop souvent contestée. Les protéger davantage face aux pressions extérieures. Et, comme projeté par le gouvernement, leur offrir des débuts de carrière moins précaires. Nous avons besoin de profs fiers, motivés, exigeants et respectés. De profs qui donnent envie d’apprendre parce qu’ils débordent eux-mêmes d’envie d’enseigner. Car une société qui ne fait plus rêver ses enseignants risque, demain, de ne plus faire rêver ses enfants. À lire aussi Rentrée scolaire : la trêve des vacances n’a pas suffi à éteindre la colère À lire aussi Ces profs victimes des réformes : « Je pourrais devoir faire jusqu’à 60 km pour compléter mon horaire » Rarement les enseignants ont exprimé un tel ressenti de mépris. L’urgence est de sortir de cette défiance et de redonner du désir et de la fierté à ce si précieux métier. Par Xavier Counasse Rédacteur en chef Le 24/08/2026 à 07:19

H uit personnes ont été transportées lundi à l’hôpital après l’accident impliquant un car autrichien et une camionnette sur l’autoroute A28 à hauteur de Wezep, aux Pays-Bas, selon un premier bilan de la police. La police indique qu’il y a également des blessés légers, sans pouvoir en préciser le nombre pour l’instant. L’autocar transportait environ cinquante personnes. D’après la police, des lycéens allemands se trouvaient à bord du bus. Vers 04h15, l’autocar et la camionnette sont entrés en collision. L’autocar a fait un tonneau et a terminé sa course sur la chaussée réservée à la circulation en sens inverse, rapportent les médias néerlandais. La camionnette a également été lourdement endommagée et s’est entièrement brisée en deux. De nombreux services de secours sont présents sur place. Le niveau d’alerte a été relevé au « code 20 », ce qui signifie que les secours se préparent à un scénario pouvant compter jusqu’à 20 blessés. Un autocar transportant une cinquantaine de personnes, dont des élèves, s’est renversé après une collision avec une camionnette sur l’autoroute A28 à Wezep, aux Pays-Bas, tôt lundi matin. Energie : l’Iran fait une découverte importante La capitale iranienne : Téhéran. - Unsplash. L ’Iran a annoncé dimanche la découverte de plus de 200 milliards de mètres cubes de gaz naturel dans le sud du pays, sur fond de guerre au Moyen-Orient, qui a notamment endommagé des infrastructures énergétiques. « De nouvelles réserves de gaz ont été découvertes dans le sud de la province de Fars », a annoncé le ministre du Pétrole, Mohsen Paknejad, cité par la télévision d’Etat, ajoutant que plus de 160 milliards de mètres cubes pourraient être extraits du champ gazier. Selon lui, ce gaz présente la particularité d’être « doux », exempt d’hydrogène sulfuré et autres composés acides, ce qui réduit à la fois les coûts d’exploitation et les coûts des opérations de développement. D’après Bloomberg, toute nouvelle production provenant du site ne devrait pas être possible avant plusieurs années. Le secteur énergétique iranien a été durement touché depuis le début de la guerre au Moyen-Orient, déclenchée fin février par des frappes américano-israéliennes contre la République islamique. Les deux pays ont notamment ciblé des installations gazières, des réservoirs de pétrole et des routes. L’Iran annonce la découverte de plus de 200 milliards de mètres cubes de gaz naturel dans la province de Fars, une réserve jugée stratégique alors que ses infrastructures énergétiques sont fragilisées par la guerre au Moyen-Orient. 1 Par AFP Le 24/08/2026 à 07:32

Turkey’s gas pivot leaves Iran with fewer cards to play. The expiry of a 25-year gas contract has exposed a shift in the Iran-Turkey energy relationship, with Ankara now enjoying more supply options while Tehran risks losing one of its most dependable export markets.

With the war quieting, Iran's hijab crackdown gathers pace again. The men who spent the war demanding control of the Strait of Hormuz have returned to demanding control of women's clothing. As the fighting subsides, Iran's hardliners are pressing to revive a hijab law the state itself suspended for fear of new protests.

British man pleads guilty to arson attack on Iran International offices. A 19-year-old British man pleaded guilty Friday to an arson offence over an April attack on offices linked to Iran International in northwest London, while a teenage co-defendant denied the more serious charge of arson being reckless as to whether life was endangered.

Trans woman prisoner says she was raped in Iran Intelligence Ministry detention. Ghazal Marzban, a transgender woman held in Tehran’s Evin prison, says she was raped after being detained by Iran’s Intelligence Ministry in 2023 and later threatened into silence, according to a letter published by the HRANA human rights news agency.

Iran Supreme Court upholds political prisoner's death sentence - rights group. Iran's Supreme Court has upheld the death sentence of 24-year-old political prisoner Arghavan Fallahi, who was convicted of “baghi,” or armed rebellion, the US-based HRANA rights group reported on Friday.

Houthis more effective Iran ally than Hezbollah, Yemen expert says. Yemen’s Houthis have become a more effective ally for Iran than Hezbollah, using Iranian support and their strategic Red Sea position to pursue both Tehran’s interests and their own agenda, Yemen analyst Mohammad al-Basha told Iran International.

Iran crude loadings plunge to one-seventh of pre-war level as blockade bites. Iranian crude loadings have fallen to about one-seventh of their pre-war level under the US naval blockade, while Chinese receipts of Iranian oil and fuel exports have also dropped sharply, tanker-tracking data reviewed by Iran International shows.

Ghalibaf's hunger warning sparks hardline backlash over showing weakness. A warning by parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf that Iran cannot endure if its people go hungry has exposed tensions in Tehran over acknowledging economic strain, with hardliners arguing that signs of weakness will encourage further US pressure.

Iran leaders sound economic alarms under Trump’s Economic D-Day. Warnings from senior Iranian officials about the cost of prolonging the war are increasingly converging with Washington’s central pressure point: whether Iran can economically sustain the conflict.

The hidden toll of Iran crackdown: disability, chronic pain, opioid dependence. The Islamic Republic may want the world to forget what happened in January, but the bodies of those who survived make that difficult.

Iran's central bank says it is not hyperinflation. Economists are not convinced. Iran's central bank governor says hyperinflation has not happened. A leading Tehran economist says it already has. Whatever it is called, the shelves tell the same story.

IRGC chief backs state broadcaster amid clashes with Pezeshkian, Ghalibaf. IRGC commander-in-chief Ahmad Vahidi praised Iran’s state broadcaster for its performance during the war with the US, throwing his weight behind an institution that has clashed with President Masoud Pezeshkian and drawn criticism from Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

Iran leader’s absence gives war camp room to shape policy. Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen or heard publicly, leaving his condition and circumstances unclear as officials govern in his name, interpret messages attributed to him and invoke his authority on questions ranging from negotiations with Washington to the conduct of the war.
Iran executes another January protest detainee. Iran executed another detainee from the January protests after the Supreme Court upheld his death sentence, the judiciary announced on Sunday.

Iranians voice economic despair as dollar hits 2 million rials. Iranians described deepening financial hardship and questioned whether economic pressure can change government policy as the dollar hit a historic 2 million rials, extending the currency's sharp decline on Sunday.

Iran security chief hints at nuclear doctrine shift after US attacks. Iran’s top security official has suggested Tehran could reconsider its longstanding rejection of nuclear weapons, arguing that US attacks on Iran have strengthened the case for acquiring an atomic bomb as a deterrent.

Persian Murakami editions race ahead of English release with AI help. Haruki Murakami’s latest novel has yet to receive an official English translation, but at least six Persian versions have already been published or are in preparation in Iran, with some translators relying on unofficial English texts and AI tools.

Will Iran bend or escalate as US launches economic war?. Iran’s leadership may see an end to the war as necessary under mounting US economic pressure, but that does not mean Tehran will heed Washington’s demands, experts say, warning that the pressure could instead drive it toward further escalation.

Iran state TV airs threat against Trump’s son Barron. Iranian state television has broadcast a segment describing efforts to reach President Donald Trump’s son Barron and referring to a $10 million reward, an unusually explicit threat against a member of the US president’s immediate family.

Cameroun : Nkolandom, chefferie et baronnie du ministre Jacques Fame Ndongo. Propriété du ministre de l’Enseignement supérieur, le Centre touristique de Nkolandom, refuge naturel et espace de préservation de la mémoire patrimoniale, situé dans le sud du pays, est surtout un lieu de rencontres discrètes entre caciques du parti présidentiel.

Bah Oury : « Il n’y a pas de régime militaire caché en Guinée ». Deux ans et demi après sa nomination, la page de la transition désormais tournée, le Premier ministre guinéen a fait sien le discours de Mamadi Doumbouya. Sans nuances. Reconduit à la tête du gouvernement, il revient sur la place de l’opposition, les disparitions, les priorités de l’exécutif et l’avenir du pays.

Pétrole : le Niger parie 1,9 milliard de dollars sur Zimar, un groupe canadien aux références introuvables. Le Niger signe avec le canadien Zimar pour construire une raffinerie à Dosso. Mais la crédibilité du groupe, introuvable sur la scène internationale, suscite des doutes jusque dans les rangs du gouvernement.

De Denis Sassou Nguesso à Abdoulaye Diop, il fut un temps où l’Algérie formait l’Afrique. L’Algérie relance sa diplomatie éducative et offre 205 bourses à des étudiants camerounais. Ce geste ravive une tradition panafricaine façonnée entre les années 1960 et 1990, pendant lesquelles nombre de dirigeants et hauts fonctionnaires du continent sont passés par l’école militaire de Cherchell ou l’ENA d’Alger.

10 choses à savoir sur Djenabou Touré, la « Madame élections » de Mamadi Doumbouya. L’ancienne patronne de la Direction générale des élections a été promue le 27 juillet à la tête du très stratégique ministère de l’Administration territoriale. Une récompense pour celle qui a mené à terme le processus électoral qui a permis à l’ancien putschiste d’obtenir l’onction des urnes.

Paul Biya, de retour au Cameroun, saura-t-il répondre aux attentes ?. Le président camerounais est arrivé à Yaoundé ce 20 août, après 74 jours passés en Suisse. Maintes fois annoncé mais toujours reporté, ce retour va-t-il permettre de débloquer les nombreux sujets en suspens ?

Blé : l’Afrique face au retour du risque de pénurie ?. Le regain de tensions entre la Russie et l’Ukraine en mer Noire, combiné aux perturbations dans le détroit d’Ormuz, mettent le marché du blé sous pression. Alors que le continent dépend des importations, les meuniers restent sur leurs gardes.

Côte d’Ivoire : les dessous de la (difficile) refonte des instances du parti au pouvoir voulue par Alassane Ouattara. La refonte du RHDP, initiée par le chef de l’État, tarde à se traduire dans les textes statutaires du parti présidentiel. Alors que de nouvelles instances ont été créées, dont un « Comité de direction », découvrez les coulisses d’une réorganisation interne complexe.

Martin Fayulu : « Félix Tshisekedi me verra sur sa route s’il change la Constitution ». L’opposant, membre de la coalition C64, met en garde le président congolais contre toute tentative de se maintenir au pouvoir, et le presse d’organiser un dialogue national inclusif. Entretien en vidéo.

Effondrement de la mine de Zamboï en Centrafrique : ce que le drame révèle des dérives du secteur de l’or au Cameroun. Un éboulement survenu sur un site minier situé à la frontière entre les deux pays, ce 18 août, a fait au moins 100 morts. Le drame relance le débat autour du contrôle défaillant de l’orpaillage au Cameroun.

Barrick, Resolute, B2Gold… La production d’or au Mali fait son « come-back ». Bamako remonte la pente dans sa production d’or malgré l’insécurité et un climat des affaires encore compliqué pour les compagnies minières.

« Ni eau, ni électricité, ni liberté » : nouvelle manifestation en Tunisie. Des centaines de Tunisiens ont manifesté le 20 août à Tunis contre Kaïs Saïed, dénonçant coupures d’électricité et pénuries d’eau. Un mouvement qui révèle la crise sociale et politique dans laquelle s’enfonce le pays.

Au Bénin, le cyberactiviste Steve Amoussou libéré après deux ans derrière les barreaux. Présenté comme la voix derrière le compte « Frère Hounvi », Steve Amoussou a été remis en liberté après avoir purgé sa peine. Sa libération intervient après une série de relaxes et de grâces décidées depuis l’élection de Romuald Wadagni.

Football en Côte d’Ivoire : la candidature unique de Yacine Idriss Diallo à la tête de la FIF n’apaise pas les tensions. Seul candidat à sa propre succession à la tête de la FIF, Yacine Idriss Diallo peine à faire l’union. Une violente altercation entre deux de ses vice-présidents révèle des fractures profondes au sein de la fédération.

Libération de deux mercenaires russes par le FLA : le rôle clé de Faure Gnassingbé entre Bamako et les rebelles. Une semaine après la libération de 82 militaires maliens détenus par le FLA et le Jnim, les indépendantistes ont libéré deux mercenaires de Wagner, ce 20 août, grâce, notamment, à l’entremise du Togo. Lomé tente activement de jouer le rôle de médiateur entre Bamako et les indépendantistes du Front de libération de l’Azawad.

Alain Ebobissé (Africa50) : « L’Afrique doit mobiliser ses propres capitaux avant d’en chercher ailleurs ». Après avoir injecté 9 milliards de dollars dans 36 projets à travers 34 pays africains, Africa50 souhaite porter ses actifs sous gestion à 5 milliards de dollars d’ici à 2030. Alain Ebobissé, son directeur général, dessine les contours de la décennie à venir.

Malgré le choc de l’AES, la banque de la Cedeao parvient à changer d’échelle. Entrée de la BAD au capital, diversification des bailleurs, gestion du choc de l’AES… La banque de développement régionale semble amorcer une nouvelle phase, comme en témoigne le relèvement récent de sa note par Moody’s.

Crise de Ceuta : l’Espagne peut-elle vraiment utiliser la carte énergétique contre le Maroc ?. La crise migratoire intervenue à Ceuta a tendu les relations entre Madrid et Rabat. Dans ce bras de fer, l’Espagne dispose d’un levier non négligeable : elle est un fournisseur de premier plan en gaz, pétrole et électricité du royaume. Décryptage.

Aux origines de la divination marocaine. Si l’islam condamne fermement la pratique de la sorcellerie, il reconnaît son existence et a intégré une part de magie. Au Maroc, pays multiculturel de tradition soufie, confrérique et maraboutique, cette magie semble avoir pris une ampleur inédite.

Cameroun : Bagofit Sun City, le bastion de luxe de Joseph Le dans l’Est. Patron du RDPC dans la région de l’Est, le ministre Joseph Le a fait du complexe hôtelier qu’il possède dans son village natal l’épicentre de son influence politique.

Paul Biya de retour au Cameroun, Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé en médiateur, l’heure de vérité pour Bassirou Diomaye Faye… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur le retour de Paul Biya au Cameroun, décrypte le rôle de Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé dans la libération de deux mercenaires russes par le FLA, analyse la bataille politique de Bassirou Diomaye Faye après sa rupture avec Ousmane Sonko, se penche sur le redémarrage de la production d’or au Mali et examine les fragilités du modèle social marocain.

La Fabrique de l’info : pourquoi certains articles de Jeune Afrique sont anonymes. Nous faisons parfois le choix de ne pas apposer de signature à certains de nos articles. Il s’agit d’une pratique délibérée, destinée à protéger journalistes et sources dans des contextes à haut risque.

Unesco : pourquoi l’Afrique ne parvient pas à sortir ses trésors naturels de la liste des sites en péril. Le continent compte relativement peu de sites naturels inscrits au patrimoine mondial de l’Unesco, mais est surreprésenté parmi ceux classés « en péril ». Du parc de la Garamba en RDC à celui du Djoudj au Sénégal, décryptage en infographies des menaces qui pèsent sur les joyaux naturels du continent.

États-Unis – Afrique : le Sénat américain a évité le pire sur l’Agoa, sans pour autant dissiper l’incertitude. Pierre angulaire des relations commerciales entre Washington et l’Afrique, l’Agoa vient d’être prolongé jusqu’en 2028. Mais sa refonte, promise depuis des mois, se fait toujours attendre.

RDC : « Plus personne ne doute que Tshisekedi a envie d’un troisième mandat ». En RDC, la tentation du troisième mandat plane sur la vie politique interne. Dialogue national, loi référendaire, opposition divisée : dans la Semaine de Jeune Afrique sur RFI, François Soudan décrypte un rapport de force favorable pour l’instant au président, Félix Tshisekedi.

Voyage dans l’univers de la magie marocaine. Créatures surnaturelles de l’ombre, transes et sacrifices, potions magiques, le Maroc est un patchwork de croyances occultes et ésotériques qui traverse toutes les classes sociales, jusqu’au Palais. Exploration d’un univers aussi sombre que fascinant.

L’idée qui a attiré 100 millions de dollars : l’inspirant pari de cette étudiante ghanéenne. À 22 ans, Nana Barwuah a fondé Afrovest, une plateforme qui met en relation des entreprises africaines et des investisseurs internationaux. En quelques mois, elle a agrégé plus de 100 millions de dollars de besoins de financement.

Mali : le cercle restreint d’Alghabass Ag Intalla, l’architecte de l’alliance entre rebelles et jihadistes. La libération de soldats maliens par le FLA marque un changement de stratégie du groupe rebelle. Mais Alghabass Ag Intalla, toujours maître de Kidal, n’entend pas remettre en cause l’alliance qu’il a scellée avec les jihadistes du Jnim. Entre fidèles et alliés de circonstance, cartographie du réseau sur lequel s’appuie le chef de guerre.
Mali : libération d’une vingtaine de soldats détenus par le FLA. La junte et le Front de libération de l’Azawad (FLA) ont procédé à des échanges de prisonniers dimanche 23 août.

Togo : les dessous du remaniement à la tête de l’armée et des renseignements. Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé a remanié en profondeur son appareil sécuritaire, le 17 août. Une refonte dictée autant par la menace jihadiste dans le nord du pays que par la volonté du président du Conseil de consolider sa mainmise sur l’armée.

Ceuta : l’Espagne ouvre des centres d’hébergement pour 1 800 migrants face à l’urgence humanitaire. Quelque 72 000 migrants avaient franchi la frontière lors d’un afflux sans précédent et meurtrier vers ce territoire espagnol en Afrique du Nord, les 30 et 31 juillet.

Ebola en RDC : l’OMS déploie 70 000 doses du vaccin Ervebo. Le vaccin est homologué contre la souche Zaïre du virus, mais pas contre la souche Bundibugyo qui sévit actuellement dans le pays. Il pourrait toutefois offrir une certaine protection.

En Zambie, irrégularités et violences postélectorales menacent un pays coutumier des alternances démocratiques. Visé par des « menaces », le chef de l’opposition, Brian Mundubile, arrivé en deuxième position lors du scrutin présidentiel du 13 août, se terre depuis plusieurs jours dans les locaux des Nations unies. Lors d’un raid de l’armée à son domicile, un député de son parti a été tué.

Au Nigeria, plus de 50 morts après le chavirement d’un bateau surchargé. L’accident s’est produit jeudi en début de journée dans le nord-ouest du pays. Les recherches se poursuivent, selon le porte-parole de l’Agence nationale de gestion des situations d’urgence de la région.

Le calvaire judiciaire d’Onsi Abichou, un Franco-Tunisien cinq fois acquitté et toujours en prison à Tunis. Poursuivi pour trafic de stupéfiants, le Franco-Tunisien a été condamné en 2008 à la prison à perpétuité. Innocenté ensuite par plusieurs cours en Tunisie, il a pourtant été de nouveau placé en détention en août 2021 dans la capitale tunisienne.

Ebola en RDC : l’épidémie progresse « de façon exponentielle » et dépasse 2 500 morts, alerte l’ONU. Face à une épidémie sans précédent, la riposte contre Ebola en RDC est freinée par le manque de moyens et la défiance de la population, alors que des essais de vaccin sont en cours.

En Tunisie, la contestation ne prend pas malgré une dégradation du niveau de vie. Jeudi soir, quelques centaines de personnes ont manifesté à Tunis contre le pouvoir du président Kaïs Saïed. Une faible mobilisation qui s’explique autant par le climat répressif que par les divisions de l’opposition.

Les ventes décevantes de Boualem Sansal malgré un battage médiatique hors norme. Parue le 2 juin, « La Légende », publiée chez Grasset, a été vendue à 48 000 exemplaires. Hachette Livre avait accordé un à-valoir exceptionnel de 1 million d’euros à l’auteur.

Au large de la Somalie, un cargo turc rempli d’armes arraisonné par des pirates. Le « Lutuf » faisait route vers Mogadiscio lorsqu’il a été capturé, lundi 17 août. La Turquie, premier partenaire sécuritaire de la Somalie, conduit des frappes contre les pirates pour tenter de récupérer la cargaison.

Au Caire, la longue restauration d’un mausolée soufi : « Ce type de projet ne doit pas s’adresser aux seuls touristes ». Depuis cinq ans, au Caire, l’ONG américaine World Monuments Fund s’emploie à faire renaître de ses ruines un complexe religieux du XVIᵉ siècle édifié par le maître soufi Ibrahim Al-Gulshani. Cette restauration vise aussi à redynamiser ce quartier médiéval méconnu de la capitale égyptienne et à y attirer davantage de touristes.

En Guinée, le retour de vacances de Mamadi Doumbouya ne suffit pas à faire taire les doutes sur sa capacité à tenir le pouvoir. Le départ en congés du président guinéen, début août, s’est accompagné de mystérieuses assurances de l’armée quant à sa loyauté. L’institution est actuellement traversée par des tensions.

« Avant, on voyait ça comme un sport de Blancs » : en Afrique du Sud, l’engouement toujours plus important autour de l’équipe nationale de rugby. Les Springboks affrontent à domicile les All Blacks néo-zélandais, samedi 22 août. Le premier d’une série de trois matchs très attendus. En dix ans, l’équipe nationale est parvenue à fédérer un large public, exauçant le rêve porté par Nelson Mandela en 1995.

Journalistes français détenus au Togo : Lomé affirme disposer d’« indices graves et concordants » à leur encontre. Arrêtés à la fin de juillet alors qu’ils tournaient un documentaire dans le nord du pays, les deux réalisateurs français sont poursuivis pour de supposées fausses déclarations liées à leur visa.

En Sierra Leone, les habitants des bidonvilles piégés par la montée de l’océan : « On est encerclés par la mer et par des torrents de pluie et d’eaux usées ». A Freetown, les précipitations et les marées transforment les quartiers proches de l’océan en vastes zones inondables. Faute d’équipements, des dizaines de milliers d’habitants vivent dangereusement au rythme des crues.

La République démocratique du Congo et les combattants du M23 annoncent une feuille de route pour les pourparlers de paix. Un calendrier précis des négociations a été établi entre la RDC et le M23, marquant une nouvelle étape dans le processus de paix sous médiation internationale.

Naufrage en Méditerranée : 12 migrants sont morts au large de la Tunisie. Un bateau transportant 15 migrants tunisiens a fait naufrage dans la nuit de vendredi à samedi. Une seule personne a été secourue et deux autres sont toujours portées disparues.

Guinée : 30 morts dans l’éboulement d’une décharge à Conakry après de fortes pluies. Le gouvernement avait annoncé ces derniers jours des opérations d’expulsion et de sécurisation des emprises autour de la décharge à cause des risques d’éboulement.

Minerais critiques : comment l’Afrique cherche à rééquilibrer le rapport de force avec les pays extracteurs. Une quinzaine de pays africains, producteurs de cobalt, de manganèse ou de lithium, ont décrété des embargos ou des quotas depuis 2023, pour contraindre les opérateurs extérieurs à investir localement dans la transformation de ces minéraux.

Le canal de Suez, naissance et mort d’un mythe colonial, promesse d’un Orient où se mêlent aventure et fortune. « Suez, canal historique » (1/6). En 1869, la création d’un axe maritime permettant de relier la Méditerranée et la mer Rouge, exploité par les Français et les Britanniques, fascine l’Europe. D’abord symbole d’oppression coloniale pour le peuple égyptien, la voie d’eau devient un instrument d’émancipation quand le président Nasser annonce sa nationalisation, il y a tout juste soixante-dix ans, le 26 juillet 1956.

SOS Méditerranée alerte sur la hausse des violences en mer contre les migrants et les navires de sauvetage. L’ONG a recensé entre juin et juillet, à sept reprises au moins, des navires « liés à des acteurs libyens » et des « groupes armés », qui se sont approchés « à grande vitesse » de bateaux, ou les ont suivis des heures durant.

Iranian parliamentary committee approves provision to charge ships in Hormuz Iranian parliament advanced a provision in a draft law on Sunday allowing Tehran to charge ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission approved Article 3 of its "Strategic Action to Ensure the Security and Progress of the Strait of Hormuz" plan, Iran's IRNA news agency reported. Based on the article, a fee will be charged for services "including maritime, environmental, fueling under special conditions, insurance, safety, and other services provided in the Strait of Hormuz." Committee spokesperson Hassan Qashqavi said the fees would be collected from vessels belonging to countries permitted to pass through the strait and paid in Iranian rials or another currency. He added that the draft legislation takes into account the rights of states bordering the Strait. "The Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz have their own rules and conditions, and in this regard, after accepting the 1982 Convention on the Law of the Sea, Oman immediately issued a political declaration emphasizing that the provisions of this convention should not violate the country's national sovereignty and national security," the article said. The draft law will now go to a full vote in parliament on its provisions and overall passage. If approved, it will then go to the Guardian Council, which checks it for compliance with the Constitution and Islamic principles. Before the war, passage through the Strait of Hormuz was free, but Iran now insists on charging fees. The US rejects the imposition of such fees, while President Donald Trump recently posted a map on social media, labelling the Strait of Hormuz as "new US territory."

Trump hits back at Canada after retaliatory tariffs announcement. US President Donald Trump hit back at Canada on Sunday after Prime Minister Mark Carney announced retaliatory tariffs on the United States following a breakdown in trade negotiations. “Canada wants the benefits of being a state, without being one!!!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs. No more!!!” he said. Carney said on Saturday that new Canadian tariffs would take effect on September 8, notably targeting the US steel and dairy industries. New 50 per cent US tariffs impacting about $20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5pc of Canadian exports to the US, came into force on Saturday. Impacted products range from hockey sticks to cement. “You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” Carney said a day earlier. New Canadian tariffs will notably target the US steel and dairy industries and take effect on September 8. More details would come next week, Carney said. Trump had previously said Washington “should be able to have a deal with Canada,” citing his “good relationship” with Carney. But on Saturday, Canada’s prime minister said Trump set conditions that were ultimately unacceptable even though earlier talks had been positive. “In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair and undermined the net benefits for Canada, and called into question the reliability of any deal,” Carney said in Ottawa. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered, and we will not give what they’ve asked.” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told the New York Times on Saturday that the US had offered to reduce its tariffs on steel, aluminium and autos, as well as eliminate a recently imposed tariff on Canadian lumber. Greer said those measures would have given Canada “the most preferential treatment of any trading partner,” according to the Times. Greer told Fox News on Saturday that Washington was “moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation.” He said no new talks were planned with Canadian negotiators. A senior US official characterised this week’s talks in Washington as candid and not acrimonious.

Spantik Peak mission to retrieve body of Pakistani climber halted amid heavy snowfall. GILGIT: Snowfall at Spantik Peak on Sunday halted efforts to retrieve the body of Pakistani climber Dr Asma Mushtaq, who died while descending the 7,027m peak in Gilgit-Baltistan’s Shigar district. 34-year-old Dr Mushtaq died at an altitude of around 6,250 metres on Thursday while descending from the summit of Spantik — also known as Golden Peak — after suffering from high-altitude sickness. Her body is currently at Camp 3. High-altitude sickness encompasses a range of pulmonary and cerebral conditions caused by hypoxia, or oxygen deprivation, due to rapid ascent and inadequate acclimatisation to high altitudes. Baltistan Division Commissioner Kamal Khan told Dawn that the rescue team of six high-altitude porters had reached Camp 2 and had attempted to start their mission towards Camp 3, but were forced to retreat back to Base Camp due to heavy rain and snow. “Due to continuous heavy snowfall and extremely strong winds, conditions have become very dangerous and risky,” he said. “The rescue team could not safely remain at Camp 2, therefore, the entire rescue team had to turn back.” He said that the team had now reached Base Camp safely and that further rescue efforts would be considered when the weather conditions improved. “The mission is being undertaken under extremely challenging high-altitude and weather conditions, and the safety of the recovery team remains a priority,” he said. According to a press release issued by the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) General Secretary Ayaz Shigri on Saturday, Dr Mushtaq’s body remains at approximately 6,400m. “The recovery team departed yesterday (i.e. Friday) and reached Camp 2 today (Saturday), but operations have been halted due to heavy snowfall,” the statement said. “The team has been advised to return to Base Camp and wait for a suitable weather window.” Approval for a mercy mission for helicopter rescue on humanitarian grounds was also in progress, with the support of the Pakistan Army, it added. The ACP statement noted that the recovery operation, consisting of climbers from different teams, was being coordinated by Dr Mushtaq’s own expedition company, in coordination with institutions including the tourism department, local government and ACP. “It was earlier reported that Dr Asma suffered from high-altitude sickness after summiting,” the press release said. “The circumstances surrounding her death, as well as the conduct and response of the expedition company, will be fully investigated once the teams are safely down and her body has been recovered.” Any necessary action would follow the findings of that investigation, it added. View this post on Instagram It also clarified ACP’s role in the venture, stating that the club was Pakistan’s national federation for mountaineering and sport climbing and not a rescue organisation with dedicated resources. Search, rescue and other relevant activities depended upon government resources, it noted, while regretting that Pakistan currently lacked a dedicated and properly established high-altitude rescue system. The ACP said that under the new leadership of the club, it was working with the relevant authorities to help with the development of an effective rescue framework and support improvements to the country’s mountaineering infrastructure. “Please refrain from spreading misinformation or making unverified claims about the recovery operation,” the club requested, noting that the safe and dignified recovery of Dr Mushtaq’s body was the priority. Shigri told Dawn that misinformation was being spread about the delay in the recovery of the body. He said that efforts were being made to recover the body from the peak and transport it to the base camp so that it could be airlifted via helicopter, pointing out that helicopters could not retrieve the body from altitudes over 6,000m. “Only the ground rescue team can bring down the body from the peak to base camp,” he said, noting that a six-member local team was making efforts in this regard. “Initially, certain confusions arose regarding the remuneration demanded by the high-altitude porters for undertaking the body recovery operation, which resulted in a delay in commencement of the recovery mission,” Khan told Dawn . According to the commissioner, no agreement had been signed between the tour operator and the mountaineer, and no insurance had been arranged for helicopter evacuation. The matter was subsequently taken up through the joint intervention and coordination of the Baltistan division civil administration, the tourism department, the GB government, EV-K2-CNR — an Italian NGO paying the expenses of the ground rescue team — and the ACP, he said. “Through their coordinated efforts, the matter was amicably resolved, and the required arrangements were finalised,” he added. Earlier, the commissioner had told Dawn that the tour operator had violated mountaineering rules by not arranging for the recovery team to retrieve Dr Mushtaq’s body from Spantik Peak and for helicopters to airlift the body from base camp to Skardu. “Under the rules, if a ground rescue team or helicopter is needed, the tour operator is responsible to arrange a rescue team and pay insurance for helicopter,” he said. The commissioner added that the operator had not conducted a briefing or debriefing either, which he said was mandatory under the Mountaineering Rules 1999. However, Khan rejected the “wrongful” impression that the recovery mission was delayed by the operator’s negligence, noting that the division and district administrations had arranged the ground team soon after the incident with an NGO paying the expenses. The Pakistan Army also agreed to provide a helicopter to airlift the body from the base camp to Skardu on humanitarian grounds. He said the mission depended on the weather: “If the weather allows, the rescue team will bring the body down to base camp, and army helicopters will airlift it from the base camp to Skardu.” Experts say bringing a body down from a high-altitude peak, particularly from above 6,000m, is an extremely risky and challenging task. In many cases, bodies at such extreme altitudes are left and buried under the snow rather than being brought down. Sajid Sadpara buried the body of his father, renowned Pakistani mountaineer Ali Sadpara , at around 8,000m on K2 in 2021. GB tourism department officials requested that people consider the risks and circumstances carefully before making comments about Dr Mushtaq’s case. Information Minister Ataullah Tarar also shared the update on his X account. He further stated, “Heli has been authorised and coordination has been done between [the] GB government and Force Commander Northern Areas. Alternate arrangements are also in place. Whatever can be done in these circumstances will be done,” he wrote, adding that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was being “kept updated on the situation. According to her social media profiles, Mushtaq was originally from Lahore and worked as a UK-based doctor specialising in obstetrics and gynaecology. Away from her medical profession, she was a passionate traveller, vlogger and mountaineer who actively documented her expeditions on social media. She completed a successful winter ascent of the 4,076-metre Musa ka Musallah peak and was associated with expeditions to Rupal and Arandu. In a 2024 post seeking K2 sponsorship, she described herself as “a doctor and mountaineer”. Broad Peak operation remains halted amid bad weather Meanwhile, due to continued bad weather conditions, helicopters were unable to fly to Broad Peak to airlift the body of US climber Sarah Mallory Geis from the base camp after the deadly avalanche that killed a 10-member expedition. The body of US climber was recovered by three local porters voluntarily from Broad Peak (8,047m) on Friday, 22 days after she went missing in a deadly avalanche . Local volunteers have moved the body to Broad Peak basecamp. Shigri said that as the weather improved, the body of the US climber would be airlifted to Skardu via Pakistan Army helicopters. Geis was among the 10 members of an expedition that went missing on July 30 after a deadly avalanche on Broad Peak. The avalanche struck on July 30, cutting off contact with the international expedition led by world-renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja on Broad Peak, one of the world’s highest mountains. Purja’s company later confirmed there were no survivors . Shigri said that nine of the climbers, including Purja and Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi , had so far been recovered and handed over to families. He added that the search for the tenth deceased member, Nawang Thindu Sherpa, would continue. Broad Peak is the world’s 12th highest mountain, located in the Karakoram range, and is regarded as one of the toughest and most technical climbs of all the 8,000-metre-plus ascents. It was first summited in 1957 by an Austrian team.

PTI demands Imran's CT angiography be conducted at Shifa International Hospital. ISLAMABAD: Following reports that jailed PTI founder Imran Khan could not undergo a recommended computed tomography angiography (CTA) during a hospital visit this week, his party condemned the authorities over their “continued failure” to carry out the procedure and demanded that it be immediately conducted at Shifa International Hospital. When the PTI founder was brought to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) in the early hours of Friday for an eye procedure and other diagnostic examinations, doctors recommended a CTA of the heart, but hospital staff reportedly said the facility was unavailable. After other tests, he was subsequen­tly shifted back to Adiala jail, reportedly without under­going the CTA, which can help identify coronary blo­ckages and assess the risk of a heart attack. Sources told Dawn the Cardiac Centre’s conventional angiography facility at Pims was different from CTA. While conventional angiography involves inserting a catheter into a blood vessel, CTA is performed using a CT scanner and does not require puncturing a vein. Doctors pointed out that a 128-slice CT scanner had been operational in Pims’ radiology department since March 2022 and was capable of performing CTA. The test is generally conducted by radiologists on the recommendation of clinicians. A senior doctor said the patient should therefore have been referred to radiology department. Taking notice of the reports, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday formed an inquiry committee, headed by the establishment division secretary, to establish facts and fix responsibility. On Sunday, PTI Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram, in a written message to Dawn , reiterated the PTI’s demand to move Imran to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad without any delay — which the Supreme Court had also directed on August 18. Akram also cited details submitted to the court, saying a medical board of the government had examined Imran on August 10 while a Pims cardiologist had already recommended CT Coronary Angiography for him on August 1 due to fluctuating blood pressure, palpitations, headaches, restlessness and the potential risk of cardiac complications arising from his age and prolonged isolation. “Even the government’s own doctors considered this diagnostic test necessary,” Akram stated. “Yet, when Imran Khan was taken to Pims, the procedure was not performed. Hospital officials claimed that the required facility was unavailable, despite the presence of a functional CT scanner in the radiology department capable of conducting the test,” he alleged. He said these reports had “intensified concerns regarding repeated delays and apparent negligence in providing Imran Khan with timely and appropriate medical care”. “A former prime minister was taken to a government hospital in the middle of the night, assessed by doctors who recommended an essential cardiac investigation, and then returned to the Adiala jail without the test being conducted. This cannot be dismissed as an isolated administrative lapse; it reflects a deeply troubling pattern,” he added. Akram said, on the other hand, the required facilities were available at Shifa International Hospital. “But, despite the Supreme Court’s order concerning Imran Khan’s comprehensive medical examination and treatment at Shifa International, the authorities chose not to take him there and instead transferred him to a facility where the CT Coronary Angiography was ultimately not conducted,” he rued. “When the necessary facilities were available at Shifa International, deliberately taking Imran Khan to a hospital where the required facilities for the procedure were not available raises a grave and unavoidable question: was the decision made in advance to prevent the CTA from being conducted?” he asked. “The authorities must explain why he was not taken to the facility specifically identified for his medical care and why he was sent to a hospital where the recommended test could not be performed.” Akram rejected the government’s assertions that Imran had been receiving adequate medical care. Regarding the prime minister’s decision to constitute an inquiry committee following reports of the failure to conduct Imran’s CTA, he said the move raised “serious questions as to why the medically recommended test was not conducted in the first instance. Why coordination between the cardiology and radiology departments had failed, and why Imran Khan was not taken to Shifa International despite the availability of the required facilities there”. He demanded that Imran’s CTA be immediately conducted at Shifa International Hospital under the supervision of independent specialists and the former premier’s personal physicians. Akram also called for the “prompt disclosure of his (Imran’s) complete medical records, reports and diagnostic results to his family, personal doctors and legal team”. Moreover, the Supreme Court’s August 18 decision should be fully implemented in letter and spirit and a transparent and independent investigation should be conducted to determine why Imran was taken to Pims instead of Shifa International and why his CTA was not conducted, Akram demanded. “Imran Khan’s heart health cannot be subjected to political calculations, administrative excuses or further delay,” Akram declared. “Political victimisation must never be permitted to endanger a human life through the denial or postponement of essential medical care. The decision to take him to a facility where the required test was not conducted, despite the availability of the necessary facilities at Shifa International, has created serious concerns that the procedure was intentionally prevented,” he alleged. “The government and all relevant authorities will bear full responsibility for any further deterioration in his condition,” Akram warned. Imran’s hospital transfer saga The PTI has been raising concerns over Imran’s health since his eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) — came to light in late January. He has been taken to Pims multiple times for treatment since. On Tuesday, the Supreme Court ordered the government to shift Imran to Shifa International Hospital within two days for examination and treatment by a multidisciplinary medical board. A three-member bench headed by Justice Shahid Waheed and comprising Justices Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Ishtiaq Ibr­ahim issued the interim directions on petitions seeking Imran’s hospitalisation, access to personal physicians and family members and provision of his medical record to his family. The court also ordered that Dr Uzma Khan and Dr Faisal Sultan — Imran Khan’s personal physician — be present during the medical check-up by a medical board. At the same time, Imran’s family members, PTI members and lawyers associated with him were barred from disclosing his health condition or medical reports to the media or public until the next hearing. The next day, the government filed a review plea against the court’s order to shift Imran to the private hospital, arguing that the directive was discriminatory and issued in violation of prison rules and principles of natural justice. However, the SC had returned the plea on Thursday with the objection that the contents of the affidavit and facts, along with the review petition filed under Article 188 of the Constitution, had not been properly drawn up and that one of the paper books was not in order. The same night, elaborate arrangements were put in place in and around Shifa International Hospital, and all signs pointed to the PTI founder being brought there, in compliance with the Supreme Court order. However, it became clear on Friday morning that Imran had been taken to Pims for a check-up and then subsequently transported back to prison. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar blamed “the security situation created by PTI workers on the way to and outside Al Shifa Hospital” for the diversion. In a post on X, he said, “In the light of the SC’s order, the prisoner was taken to the hospital under appropriate security arrangements during the night between August 20 and 21. “A team of qualified doctors, including an ophthalmologist, a cardiologist, and a physician, conducted a detailed examination of him and declared him medically fit,” he said. The PTI rejected the allegation and flayed the government for “flouting” the SC order. Later, the Pims administration said that two specialists from Shifa Inter­national Hospital participated in Imran’s eye assessment, while other exa­minations were carri­­ed out by the concerned Pims specialists. “The clinical input ari­sing from the ophthalmological assessment was taken into account alongside findings of the investigations conducted at Pims,” the statement said. Meanwhile, the government on Thursday filed a fresh review petition against the SC’s Aug 18 order. The Islamabad chief commissioner again filed the plea, saying that his office had a direct, substantial and legally protected interest in the matter and that the Aug 18 order adversely affected its constitutional authority.

Hina Javed murder case: Rawalpindi court sends husband, servant on 3-day physical remand. RAWALPINDI: A duty magistrate in Rawalpindi on Sunday remanded the husband and servant of Hina Javed in police custody for three days in her murder case. Hina was found dead in the washroom of her apartment in Askari Apartments in Rawalpindi on Thursday evening. Police said that the body bore signs of torture, with a wire fastened around her neck and tied to the shower rod. They detained her husband and a servant in relation to the case. Today, the suspects were produced before a duty magistrate by police, who sought their remand for further investigation. The court granted the Civil Lines police their three-day physical remand, directing authorities to submit a progress report after the remand’s completion. The FIR A first information report of the case was registered on Aug 20 at the Civil Lines police station under Sections 302 (premeditated murder) and 34 (common intention) of the Pakistan Penal Code. The complainant, Hina’s brother, Fahid Javed, alleged in the FIR that his sister had been murdered by her husband, her father-in-law and their domestic servant. Fahid told police that he received a telephone call from his sister’s father-in-law at 6:53pm on Thursday, informing him of an emergency at their residence. He said he rushed to the apartment with other family members and arrived there at 7:23pm. He claimed that when he arrived at the residence, he found his sister’s body in the bathroom. The complainant further alleged that his sister had been subjected to “severe torture and mistreatment” by her husband. He also claimed that she might have been administered a poisonous substance before her death. In his complaint, Fahid said Hina had married the suspect in November 2025. An initial postmortem examination indicated a strangulation mark around her neck, an injury below her right lip and bleeding. On Sunday, police sources told Dawn the cause of death could be ascertained with finality after the Punjab Forensic Science Agency’s (PFSA) report was received. The sources said the role of Hina’s father-in-law in the case was also yet to be determined and that he was being questioned and asked not to leave the city. Meanwhile, they added, a seven-member team, headed by Rawalpindi Senior Superintendent of Police (Investigation) Saifullah had been formed to investigate the case. The sources also said that mobile phones of the victim and three of her family members had been taken into custody for investigation.

Nordic nations say they have lost confidence in Infantino and Fifa governance. Six Nordic football associations delivered a united blow to Fifa President Gianni Infantino on Sunday, declaring they had lost confidence in his leadership while demanding sweeping governance reforms at world football’s governing body. The ​six Nordic Fifa members — Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and the Faroe Islands — met in ‌Helsinki and issued a rare joint statement backing calls for Infantino’s resignation from three major regional confederations. They also supported demands for an independent investigation into his controversial proposal to sell a stake in events like the World Cup to private equity ​investors, a plan that was quickly abandoned in the face of global backlash. “The six Nordic football ​associations have lost confidence in Fifa’s president and are concerned about the organisation’s governance ⁠and decision-making at the highest level,” they said in a statement. “The Nordic football associations stand united with ​UEFA and support the measures that the organisation and its national member associations have jointly proposed. “We expect Fifa ​to provide binding guarantees that the organisation’s governance or competitions will never again be opened up to private ownership.” Reuters has contacted Fifa for comment on the statement. On Friday, Denmark’s football association (DBU) vowed to find a credible alternative to Infantino in next year’s ​election. Infantino is under pressure from three confederations to resign, including Europe’s UEFA, Asia’s AFC and Concacaf, which represents North ​and Central America and the Caribbean. The sport’s regional powerhouses have also discussed a potential vote of no confidence against the Fifa ‌chief. “We ⁠also support the demand made by AFC, Concacaf and UEFA that a fully independent external investigation into the events surrounding the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal be established,” the Nordic FAs added. “We also call on Fifa to initiate a comprehensive and independent review of its governance framework to determine whether it ensures the independence, checks ​and balances, transparency and accountability ​that were intended when ⁠Fifa adopted its reform programme in 2016.” Infantino, who is seeking a fourth term until 2031 at next year’s election, is in the Dominican Republic this weekend ​, where he met with officials of the Caribbean Football Union. Concacaf President Victor Montagliani had ​asked Infantino to ⁠stay away from a youth football tournament in the country, saying his presence would overshadow the event. “This meeting of the Presidents of CFU takes place in the environment of (a) Under-14 youth tournament in the region, which actually ⁠is one ​of those tournaments that can take place thanks (to) the Fifa Forward programme,” Infantino said. “So, even more so, a reason to be proud to be here. And happy, as well, because it’s important to ​engage, to have a dialogue, to express views and opinions.”

Dar arrives in UK ahead of official visit starting on Monday. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar reached the United Kingdom on Sunday, ahead of a four-day official visit beginning on Monday, the Foreign Office (FO) said. Pakistan’s High Commissioner to the UK Tipu Usman received him at London’s Heathrow airport, FO added. Earlier, FO said that during the visit, DPM Dar will meet the UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) Minister of State for Pakistan Stephen Doughty, as well as other senior members of the government. “He will also meet with the secretary-general of the International Maritime Organisation to discuss the issue of Pakistani crew members held by Somali pirates aboard the MT Honour 25 oil tanker, in addition to a meeting with the Commonwealth Secretary-General, Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey,” FO said. It added that Dar is also expected to meet British parliamentarians and representatives of the Pakistani diaspora in the UK. The visit comes after the two countries agreed to intensify bilateral trade engagement and strengthen business-to-business cooperation in July. The two sides had explored upgrading an existing Trade Dialogue into a more structured economic and trade framework. In June, Pakistan and the UK had agreed to enhance cooperation in counterterrorism, combating illegal migration and human smuggling, institutional collaboration and police training. This understanding was reached as the Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi met British Minister of State for the Middle East, South Asia and the UN Hamish Falconer.

ISI chief meets Bahrain's crown prince, discusses regional and international developments: report. Inter-Services Intelligence chief Lt Gen Muhammad Asim Malik held a meeting with Bahrain’s crown prince, Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, on Sunday and discussed ways to enhance cooperation, as well as the latest regional and international developments, according to Bahrain’s state news agency. Bahrain News Agency reported that the meeting was held at the official royal residence, Riffa Palace. The report said the crown prince, who is also the commander of Bahrain’s armed forces, “affirmed the depth of the bilateral relations” that “continue to strengthen due to a shared commitment to furthering ties and achieving common goals” between the two countries. He emphasised the importance of continuing efforts to deepen joint coordination across various fields, contributing to the mutual prosperity and growth of both countries, the report said. It added that ways to enhance cooperation, the latest regional and international developments, and matters of mutual interest also came under discussion. The crown prince highlighted Pakistan’s “critical role, alongside its allies, in strengthening the foundations of regional security and stability”. For his part, the report said, Lt Gen “expressed his gratitude” the crown prince for his commitment to further develop bilateral ties and “wished the Kingdom of Bahrain continued progress and prosperity”. Bahrain’s minister of the prime minister’s court, finance minister, deputy interior minister, deputy national security adviser and Supreme Defence Council deputy secretary general also attended the meeting, the report said. Around two weeks ago, Bahrain’s Foreign Minister Dr Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani had also held a phone call with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar to congratulate Pakistan on the signing of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. The Foreign Office had said that the Bahraini foreign minister had also expressed intentions to visit Pakistan in the near future during the phone call. In June, the commander of Bahrain’s National Guard, General Shaikh Mohammad bin Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa, had met Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff (COAS) Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir at the General Headquarters in Rawalpindi and discussed the strengthening of military collaboration with Pakistan. The Bahraini official had also met Pakistan’s air and naval chiefs during his visit to Pakistan.

Sindh govt to seek judicial commission to review Mir Raza murder probe; family to move SHC against decision. The Sindh government said on Sunday it would be asking the chief justice of the provincial high court to establish a judicial commission to determine whether the investigation in the Mir Raza Ali murder case was being conducted impartially and in accordance with the law. But, soon after the announcement, the counsel for Ali’s family raised objections and said they would approach the Sindh High Court on Monday against the decision. The Sindh government’s decision came days after Ali’s parents approached Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah, requesting that he directly supervise the investigation. His parents, Mir Hussain and Mariam, wrote a letter to the Sindh chief minister through their lawyer Jibran Nasir, alleging that the investigation continued to suffer as the probe team “appears to focus on perpetuating the false narrative of the death of the deceased by suicide”. A statement issued by the Sindh chief minister’s office on Sunday said their letter had been received with “compassion and the utmost seriousness”. “After carefully considering the concerns expressed by the family, the government of Sindh has decided to request the honourable chief justice of the Sindh High Court to establish a judicial commission to conduct an impartial and transparent inquiry,” the statement said. It added that the commission should determine whether the investigation in the case was being conducted impartially and in accordance with law. It should also identify any investigative angle or evidence requiring further investigation. Moreover, the commission should determine whether “any police officer, medico-legal officer or other official committed negligence, dereliction of duty, professional misconduct, suppression or manipulation of evidence, or any unlawful act, omission or cover-up”. The commission may recommend further investigation, forensic analysis and appropriate legal or departmental action wherever warranted, the statement said. “For the effective discharge of its mandate, the commission shall exercise all powers available to it under the Sindh Tribunals of Inquiry Ordinance, 1969, including the powers of a civil court to summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses, examine them on oath, and require the discovery and production of documents and other records. “All government departments, agencies and officials have been directed to extend full cooperation to the commission and provide every record, document and form of assistance sought by it. The Home Department shall provide the necessary secretariat support,” the statement read. It added that the commission should submit its report, together with its findings and recommendations, to the Sindh government within 30 days of its constitution, or within such extended period as may be allowed where necessary for a complete and fair inquiry. “The commission will be fully empowered to examine the conduct of the investigation and recommend appropriate action in accordance with law,” it said. The government also expressed solidarity with Ali’s family in this time of grief. Reacting to the provincial government’s decision, counsel for Ali’s family, Jibran Nasir, posted on X that they would move the Sindh High Court tomorrow to form a joint investigation team (JIT) and oppose the planned commission. “Forming a judicial commission without informing the family of Mir Raza, nor making the terms of reference of the inquiry public. Why are other law enforcement agencies not engaged and a JIT [is not] formed? Why is the criminal conduct of police officers not investigated? Tomorrow, the family will move the high court for JIT and to oppose the judicial commission,” he wrote on X. He pointed out that police were yet to submit an investigation report before the magistrate. “Before the submission of the police report, why has the Sindh govt announced a judicial commission? Is it because they know the outcome of the police investigation and they disagree with it?” he questioned. In a video message, Ali’s family also rejected the Sindh government’s decision. Sitting between her parents, his sister, Alishba, said they came to know about the Sindh government’s decision through the media. Raising similar objections and questions as those by Nasir, she said: “On August 24, the police are to submit their report. But if there is no report yet, on what basis are they making this decision?” “We, as a family, are not standing for this decision. We have been saying this since the beginning that we do not trust how the proceedings are going on,” she said. She said they still had not received any response to their letter to the chief minister. “We want more law enforcement and intel agencies to be a part of this; we want a JIT,” she said, adding that they would approach the court tomorrow (Monday). She said the family had also sent a message to the Sindh home minister and asked him to provide a copy of the decision. The case Ali, a 25-year-old businessman and a graduate of the Institute of Business Administration, was found dead with a gunshot wound on July 29 in bushes in Karachi’s Gulistan-i-Jauhar a day after he was reported missing. While his family was convinced that he was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, police were initially building the case around the possibility that he died by suicide. A murder charge was eventually added to the first information report (FIR) after the exhumation and a second post-mortem of Ali’s body revealed that he had suffered multiple injuries and was shot in the back, ruling out the possibility of suicide. The second autopsy was conducted after a controversy between the Karachi police surgeon and investigators over alleged loopholes in the medico-legal report regarding Ali’s first post-mortem examination. On August 6, a judicial magistrate had allowed the exhumation of the body on an application filed by Ali’s father, directing the police surgeon and the Sindh health secretary to constitute a medical board for the exhumation. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with police surgeon Dr Sumaiyya Syed as the convener. However, in the early hours of August 7, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed. But Ali’s family rejected the new board, which also resulted in the deferment of the planned exhumation on Friday. Meanwhile, the counsel for Ali’s family, Nasir accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts. The Sindh government then restored the original medical board, following which Ali’s body was exhumed on August 8. A day later, the Sindh inspector general of police’s (IG) office notified the reconstitution of the investigating team probing Ali’s death while Karachi Additional IG Azad Khan transferred the investigation into Ali’s murder to Zaman Town police station from Ferozabad Police Station, where the case was registered. The same day, the Sindh government decided to seek a judicial commission for the case’s investigation, only to defer the plan a day later after Ali’s family said they had made no such demand and had faith in the new investigation team. Letter to CM But on Wednesday, they wrote to the Sindh chief minister, expressing dissatisfaction with the probe. In their 22-page letter to Murad, which went into extensive detail about the incident and subsequent investigations, as well as the controversies surrounding the case, they stated that the “murderers and the conspirators of murder… despite public scrutiny continue to appear to exercise considerable political clout to ensure that the truth remains suppressed”. The letter said that Raza’s parents “are horrified at the level of corruption, incompetence and political influence prevalent within Sindh Police”. In the letter, Advocate Nasir, on behalf of the victim’s family, demanded the immediate suspension of police officers who were part of the original investigation team. Referring to Sindh police’s statement on Tuesday that it had ruled out suicide following the second post-mortem examination of the body, the letter questioned “why the current investigation team continues to spend time and energy analysing and re-analysing these reports rather than focusing on securing and rationalising multiple other sources of evidence”. The letter then listed 24 questions that remained unanswered in the investigation, including those concerning Raza’s communications shortly before his murder and the circumstances surrounding his death. It also raised questions about missing digital and forensic evidence. The letter further pointed out that police had not answered questions concerning the alleged actions of Raza’s business partner in the days immediately before and after his murder. “The police hierarchy has been reduced to a tool used to corrupt and later destroy the crime scene,” the letter alleged. The previous investigation team’s conduct “attracts multiple penal offences under the Pakistan Penal Code”, the letter said, specifically mentioning Section 201, for “causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen offender”, and Section 218, relating to a “public servant framing incorrect record or writing with intent” to save someone from punishment. The letter went on to propose 10 charges against the police officers concerned, including deliberate mishandling of material evidence, failure to record witness statements, deliberate manipulation of the investigation record, unlawful handling of the deceased’s devices, and “abuse of official position and concerted acts to defeat the course of investigation”, among others. The letter also proposed 13 terms of reference for a departmental inquiry against the police officers, including an inquiry into “why the former investigation team prematurely adopted and promoted the theory of suicide” and “why the investigation team failed to respond to and heed the letter of the Police Surgeon Karachi”. The letter also questioned why the special medical board had faced resistance and called for an examination into “the custody, handling and forensic examination of the deceased’s smartwatch”. It further urged the departmental inquiry to “determine whether any senior police officer, public office-holder or other person improperly influenced, directed or pressured the former investigation team to adopt, maintain or promote the suicide narrative or otherwise interfere with the investigation”. Additional input from Imtiaz

Cricket greats appeal to PM Shehbaz for Imran's medical treatment in line with SC directives. Twenty-two international cricketers, including 21 ex-captains, have written a letter to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, making an appeal for ex-Pakistani premier Imran Khan’s medical treatment in line with recent Supreme Court directives, ESPN Cricinfo reported on Sunday. On August 18, the Supreme Court directed the government to move Imran to Islamabad’s Shifa International Hospital, a private facility, within two days for examination and treatment by a multidisciplinary medical board. However, it later turned out that Imran was instead taken to the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims). Meanwhile, it was also reported that he could not undergo a recommended computed tomography angiography (CTA) at Pims as the required facilities were unavailable at the hospital. The letter written by the 22 ex-cricketers and cited by ESPN Cricinfo stated: “Pakistan’s Supreme Court ordered that Imran Khan be transferred to hospital for examination by a medical board that was to include his own personal physicians and his sister, Dr Uzma Khan. “The court also reinstated weekly family visits. These were very welcome steps.” However, the former cricketers noted, Imran’s hospital stay lasted only a few hours. “He was examined by a state-appointed team rather than the board the court had directed, declared ‘medically fit’, and returned to Adiala Jail before that board could complete its work,” the letter claimed, according to ESPN Cricinfo. The former cricketers called for: Permitting the medical board directed by the Supreme Court — including Imran’s own doctors — to complete a full and independent assessment of his health, particularly the reported loss of vision in his right eye. Honouring the weekly family visits reinstated by the court without interruption or administrative delay Providing the recommended treatment to Imran without delay following the outcome of his medical assessment The letter’s signatories included Michael Atherton, Alex Blackwell, Allan Border, Michael Brearley, Greg Chappell, Ian Chappell, Belinda Clark, Alastair Cook, Michael Gatting, Sunil Gavaskar, Lee Germon, Adam Gilchrist, David Gower, Kim Hughes, Nasser Hussain, Clive Lloyd, Kapil Dev, Arjuna Ranatunga, Andrew Strauss, Dilip Vengsarkar, Steve Waugh and John Wright. In their appeal, they said they were writing “not as politicians, but as former colleagues and rivals who share a bond forged on the cricket field“ and that they did not seek to adjudicate Pakistan’s domestic legal processes. Several of these former cricketers had called on the authorities in February as well, expressing “deep concern” about Imran’s treatment and prison conditions. The cricket greats had urged the Pakistan government to ensure immediate and adequate medical attention, dignified treatment, and unhindered access to legal processes for Imran. Imran has been in jail since August 2023, convicted in a string of cases that he says were politically driven following his ouster in a 2022 parliamentary vote. There has been much ado over his health in recent months, with him having been taken to the hospital multiple times for an eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) — that came to light in late January. Meanwhile, his party, the PTI, and the government have been engaged in a blame game , with the former accusing the latter of a lack of transparency in not ensuring appropriate treatment for Imran.

Curfew re-imposed in Balochistan’s restive Mastung tehsil. QUETTA: The Balo­chistan Home Department on Sunday again imposed an indefinite curfew in Khad Kocha Tehsil of Mastung district, citing security concerns and the need to maintain law and order and protect the lives and property of the public. The department order, which took effect at 7am, completely restricts public movement on roads and in markets in Khadkocha and its adjoining areas. The district administration and law enforcement agencies have intensified security measures in the area to prevent and promptly respond to any untoward incident. Additional law enforcement personnel have been deployed to ensure compliance, establish the writ of the state, and respond to any potential incidents. The district administration urged residents to stay indoors and cooperate with authorities. In a notification, the administration warned anyone venturing outside and violating the restrictions would do so at their own risk. The curfew will remain in force until further notice, authorities said. Earlier on July 22, authorities ordered a similar lockdown in Khad­kocha after three people were killed and five others injured in a gun attack on a Karachi-bound bus.
