Comstech chief remains defiant in face of ‘damning inquiry’. • President-ordered probe found OIC official guilty of ‘misconduct, non-compliance’ • Accused official calls inquiry ‘one-sided’, claims Presidency was ‘misused’ ISLAMABAD: An inquiry committee formed on the directives of President Asif Ali Zardari has declared the top official of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation’s (OIC) Standing Committee on Scientific and Technological Cooperation (Comstech) guilty of multiple charges of misconduct. According to the inquiry report seen by Dawn, Comstech Coordinator General Dr Iqbal Choudhry was accused of financial irregularities, violation of executive orders and non-compliance with court directives. However, the official in question has questioned the legality of proceedings against him, calling it a “one-sided inquiry”. According to the inquiry report, Dr Choudhry was initially appointed by then-president Arif Alvi in 2020 during the PTI’s tenure, and was subsequently reappointed by President Zardari for another four-year term in October 2024. Under Articles 12(2), read with 16(3) of the Comstech statute, the President of Pakistan is the appointing authority for the post of the body’s coordinator general. Comstech was created in January 1981 at the Third Islamic Summit in Makkah, Saudi Arabia. Headquartered in Islamabad, Pakistan, it aims to promote science, technology and research cooperation among OIC member states. The inquiry committee was headed by Dr Asim Hussain, the chancellor of Ziauddin University. Its members included Pakistan Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (PCSIR) Chairman Dr Syed Hussain Abidi, Ministry of Science and Technology Secretary Shahid Iqbal Baloch and its Chief Finance and Accounts Officer Muhammad Saeedullah Yousafzai. Inquiry findings The committee held that Dr Choudhry had failed to implement instructions issued by the president, terming the alleged failure “misconduct”. It also accused him of violating court orders, and failing to reply to complaints. The inquiry found that meetings of the Comstech Executive Committee had not been convened for the last four years, and that most decisions were taken by Dr Choudhry alone, terming this “maladministration”. It further maintained that expenditures had been incurred for several years without budgetary approval, which the committee declared “unauthorised and illegal”. The report recommended strict disciplinary action over the alleged misuse of Comstech funds, including expenditure allegedly made for personal benefit. The committee alleged that Dr Choudhry undertook more than 70 foreign trips over the last six years without prior approval from the president in his capacity as Comstech chairman. Some of the visits, it said, were to countries not associated with Comstech, while funds were also allegedly used to cover the travel and accommodation expenses of female associates. The report also pointed out that Dr Choudhry simultaneously held the posts of Comstech coordinator general and director of the International Centre for Chemical and Biological Sciences (ICCBS) from April 8, 2020, to Nov 12, 2024, a period of around four and a half years, despite directives from the ministry to relinquish the additional charge. The inquiry also cited complaints regarding forced resignations and dismissals of employees, a lack of transparent procedures in disciplinary proceedings, and allegations of nepotism and favouritism in recruitment. It noted that the World Academy of Sciences, Trieste, Italy, had also issued a reprimand letter to Dr Choudhry. The inquiry committee has recommended that the matter be referred to anti-corruption institutions for further investigation and appropriate action against Dr Choudhry on multiple counts of alleged misconduct. The recommendations in the inquiry report have been submitted to the competent authority for further proceedings. Official’s response When approached for comment, Dr Choudhry told Dawn he was unaware of any such report, but raised questions over the legality of the inquiry, noting that procedural requirements had not been fulfilled. He claimed that neither any complaint nor a show cause notice was shared with him, and said that there were “serious procedural flaws in this one-sided inquiry”. “You cannot do it on the basis of a fake complaint,” he remarked. He maintained that the president, in his capacity as Comstech chairman, draws his powers from OIC procedures, and could not as as head of the state take a unilateral action against an OIC body which enjoys diplomatic immunity. Alleging that the Presidency was being misused, he said any inquiry or report prepared without proof or documentation has no legal or ethical standing, and is liable to be challenged in court. CORPORATE WINDOW: The crossroads of collapse. Five years after the Taliban returned to Kabul, Afghanistan’s economic relationship with Pakistan is undergoing a structural shift. For Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, particularly Peshawar, this is not simply a bilateral trade issue. It is increasingly a question of industrial resilience and competitiveness. The clearest evidence is Afghanistan’s transit trade through Pakistan. Container traffic, which had risen to nearly 89,000 containers worth about $5 billion before the Taliban returned to power, briefly climbed to a record 102,886 containers valued at $6.7bn in FY23. It then went into reverse. Volumes fell to 54,114 containers in FY24 and 42,959 in FY25, worth $1.36bn. In FY26, they collapsed to just 11,592 containers valued at $367 million, according to customs data cited in a recent Dawn report. The numbers matter because they show that Pakistan’s October 2025 border restrictions did not create the decline; they accelerated a process that was already under way. As Afghanistan shifts imports towards Iran and Central Asia, Pakistan risks losing not only transit trade but also the industrial and commercial ecosystem built around it Kabul has been deliberately diversifying its trade routes, with Iran emerging as the most important alternative. The World Bank’s Afghanistan Economic Monitor reports that the Iranian corridor has become the backbone of Afghanistan’s import supply chain. In FY25, Iran accounted for 31.3pc of Afghan imports, while direct imports from Iran and imports transiting through Iran together represented 48.6pc of total imports. Central Asian routes are also gaining importance. This means Pakistan is losing more than transit fees. It is losing its traditional position as Afghanistan’s principal gateway to international markets. The reverse-transit trade has suffered an even sharper collapse. Afghan exports travelling through Pakistan to third markets fell from $454m in FY25 to only $7m in FY26, according to Customs data. For decades, Afghan demand supported an economic ecosystem linking Karachi’s ports with Peshawar and the border markets. Manufacturers, wholesalers, transporters, clearing agents, warehouses and financial intermediaries all benefited from the movement of goods into Afghanistan. When that flow contracts, the damage travels far beyond the customs post. Industries in KP already face high energy, financing and transport costs. A shrinking Afghan market adds another burden: weaker demand precisely when businesses need greater capacity utilisation to remain competitive. Cement, construction materials, food products, pharmaceuticals, textiles and consumer goods have traditionally found markets in Afghanistan. A sustained reduction in Afghan orders threatens manufacturers and wholesalers alike. A truck that does not cross the border means less income for a transporter. A warehouse without cargo requires fewer workers. A wholesaler with fewer Afghan customers reduces purchases from manufacturers. A factory with fewer orders cuts production. The disruption is also affecting trade of industrial inputs, for example, imports of coal from Kabul. Cross-border supply disruptions can therefore raise production costs while export demand is weakening. The situation is problematic to say the least. A manufacturer can respond to falling demand by reducing prices, production or margins. But if input costs are rising simultaneously, the options narrow sharply. The result is a loss of competitiveness, not only in Afghanistan but potentially in domestic and other export markets. The consequences extend beyond industry. Agricultural markets on both sides of the border are highly sensitive to delays because fruits and vegetables are perishable. When Torkham or Chaman is closed or severely congested, exporters cannot simply store their cargo indefinitely. Recent developments illustrate the cost. In 2025, five southern Afghan provinces that make up the country’s main grape-producing region exported 44,225 tonnes of grapes worth $13.8m; nearly 43,000 tonnes went to Pakistan, with the remainder going to Bangladesh, Iraq and India. So far in 2026, exports have fallen to just 256 tonnes, valued at about $100,000, according to a recent Associated Press report. Such losses are not confined to Afghan farmers. Pakistani transporters, commission agents, wholesalers and retailers are also affected by interruptions to cross-border commerce. At the centre of the problem is the Afghanistan-Pakistan Transit Trade Agreement (APTTA), designed to turn geography into economic opportunity. Pakistan offered Afghanistan access to seaports; Afghanistan offered Pakistan a potential land bridge towards Central Asia. But security concerns, smuggling, regulatory disputes and political tensions have steadily eroded the commercial value of that arrangement. Pakistan has legitimate concerns. Transit cargo destined for Afghanistan can be diverted into Pakistani markets, depriving the government of revenue and creating unfair competition for domestic businesses. In October 2023, Pakistan imposed a 10pc processing fee on specified categories of Afghan transit goods, including garments, footwear, machinery, blankets and textiles, as part of efforts to curb misuse of the transit system. Afghanistan, however, has legitimate commercial concerns of its own. Every additional document, financial requirement, inspection or border delay raises the cost and uncertainty of trade. If an alternative route through Iran becomes commercially viable, traders have an incentive to use it. And once a trader establishes a new supply chain, winning him back becomes considerably harder. Afghanistan will not escape the cost of this realignment. Longer routes can increase transport and logistics expenses, while Pakistan loses port activity, trucking, warehousing, customs-related business and market access. There are undoubtedly consequences for the entire Pakistan economy, but for KP the consequences are immediate. Peshawar’s traders, transporters, warehouses, clearing agents and manufacturers form an interconnected commercial ecosystem built around access to Afghanistan and, beyond it, Central Asia. The Pak-Afghan Joint Chamber of Commerce and Industry estimates that Pakistani exporters suffered about $225m in losses over eight months of this year because of restrictions and blockades. It puts Pakistan’s annual exports to Afghanistan around $1.5bn, while exports to Central Asian markets through Afghanistan at $800m a year. This is particularly disturbing for KP because geography has traditionally been its competitive advantage. Peshawar and the wider Khyber corridor were positioned to benefit from trade between Pakistan, Afghanistan and Central Asia. That advantage is now being weakened as Afghanistan diversifies its trade routes. Pakistan therefore cannot treat the collapse of Afghan transit trade solely as a security or diplomatic issue. Nor can Kabul assume that replacing Pakistani routes with Iranian and Central Asian corridors carries no economic cost. Both sides need a predictable, rules-based transit regime. ‘Grand dialogue’. THE country’s top civil and military leaders are absolutely right when they say that dialogue and development are needed to address Balochistan’s crises. But perhaps one should recall that many earlier attempts by the state to bring peace to the province were stalled or remain unimplemented. In order to truly stabilise Balochistan and bring lasting peace to this troubled province, a credible political process must begin, with the state guaranteeing that it will fully implement previous promises, as well as new agreements. While speaking at the Balochistan National Workshop in Islamabad recently, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for a “grand, frank and meaningful dialogue” to address the province’s issues. He added that the province’s people had first right over its resources. In a similar vein the chief of defence forces stressed the need for empowering Balochistan’s youth. It is certainly welcome that the rulers see the need to tackle Balochistan’s political problems through dialogue. While kinetic measures are needed to deal with immediate terrorist threats, the underlying factors fuelling discontent can only be handled through a political process. The state must keep in mind previous attempts to address the province’s problems. For example, the PPP government had in 2009 launched the Aghaz-i-Huqooq-i-Balochistan package. Despite the passage of 17 years, many of the package’s key points remain unimplemented. For example, it had proposed releasing political workers, except those involved in heinous crimes. However, over the past few months, we have seen peaceful activists rounded up and thrown in jail. Similarly, the 2009 package had sought to address the province’s socioeconomic woes; suffice it to say, social indicators in Balochistan remain miserable. The PML-N had launched a package of its own in 2015. Much of that scheme also remains unfulfilled. CPEC was similarly supposed to transform the province’s fortunes. It has not. Instead of reinventing the wheel, the state must implement what it had promised in these packages. Many of these schemes’ salient points reflect the demands of the province’s nationalist politicians. Therefore, to implement these promises in full, a grand dialogue should bring on board the province’s genuine political leadership, as well as peaceful activists, while a verifiable and transparent mechanism needs to be worked out to help implement previous and new promises. The past few months have seen a sharp spike in terrorist activity in Balochistan . The only sustainable way of addressing the insurgency is to supplement kinetic actions with a genuine political process that can, in the long-term, eliminate the underlying factors that are fuelling discontent. Published in Dawn, August 24th, 2026

Women’s leadership. PAKISTAN doesn’t fare well on indices related to gender gap and women’s empowerment. The damning statistics include the number of girls who are out of school, the wide gender digital divide, high rates of violence against women, and women’s low representation in private and public leadership positions. However, over time, there have been significant advances for Pakistani women leaders. Mohammad Ali Jinnah’s sister, Fatima Jinnah , was a key figure in Pakistan’s independence movement. She later became a presidential candidate, derided by the dictator Gen Ayub Khan. When Benazir Bhutto was elected prime minister in 1988, Pakistan became the first Muslim-majority country to be led by a woman. Pakistani women have led movements against dictators, including generals Ayub, Zia and Musharraf. Asma Jahangir was the first woman to be elected president of the Supreme Court Bar Association. Begum Naseem Wali Khan was the first woman to win a general election seat in the country. Justice Ayesha Malik is the first woman Supreme Court judge. Currently, Maryam Nawaz is the first woman chief minister in Pakistan. Trans women have also made their mark, with Aisha Mughal being the first to represent a country at a UN session. Recently, Nayyab Ali was nominated for a civilian award by the government. But despite these significant positives, the prosecution of political women in Pakistan is at an all-time high. Several women leaders of the PTI remain behind bars, including the ageing cancer survivor, Dr Yasmin Rashid, who has health issues . Since January, award-winning human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari Hazir has been in jail serving a 17-year sentence for mere tweets. Baloch women have now joined numerous men who have been forcibly disappeared; several remain in jail in politically motivated cases. The prosecution of political women in the country is at an all-time high. Do such incarcerations, cases and disappearances send an encouraging message to young girls across Pakistan? Does it motivate reluctant families to send girls to school so they can get an education and start careers? Does it motivate young lawyers to take up cases of the voiceless pro bono? Does it encourage young women to enter politics and do good for the people? The incarcerations reflect a deep-rooted patriarchy that plagues the entire system. Take, for instance, gender-based attacks against women during election campaigns. The Digital Rights Foundation documented at least 163 social media posts in the run-up to the 2024 election that included gendered disinformation against women politicians, and at least 47 posts targeting “journalists covering the elections, subjecting them to gendered insults and online trolling campaigns that included online threats of physical assault”. Deepfakes targeting women human rights defenders have become commonplace, with dehumanising content being disseminated online of women that are critical of state policies, with little to no consequences for such actions — despite Section 22 of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act that makes edited and non-consensual imagery a crime. Since the 2025 amendment to Peca , the state is an eager complainant against journalists who are critical of it. Whereas the new ability of the state to file cybercrime cases against activists, journalists and politicians is to be condemned and should be reversed; it is worth noting that the state doesn’t take cognisance of instances of harassment and vitriol on social media that lead to crimes against women and children. This includes routine cases of men mercilessly killing women for rejecting their advances and proposals. The victims include women who are public figures on social media platforms as content creators. On Aug 20, former professor and motivational speaker Faisal Asghar Imam was named in the murder case of his wife in their home, and social media was rife with testimonies of him making his students uncomfortable in class and online. The link between online misogyny and physical harm to life must not be taken lightly. When Peca was being promulgated, those of us who opposed it were labelled anti-women for opposing the law. Today, we see how women are harassed, jailed, and punished including for naming their harassers by the same law meant to protect them. The abuse of the law is not restricted to targeting women who dare to speak truth to power. Human rights lawyer Hadi Ali Chattha is currently serving a 17-year sentence for supporting his wife Imaan Mazari Hazir, with his punishment framed for the “crime” of reposting her tweets. Seemingly, men who support women related to them, they too will be punished. In our geopolitical context, targeting women in the public sphere is particularly alarming. Girls in Afghanistan are not allowed to go to school after Class 6; women are not allowed to leave their house for employment, and they cannot even sing or be heard in public. In Iran, women have been killed for simply opposing the state’s enforcement of head covering rules. In such an environment, it would be a powerful message to the neighbourhood if Pakistan has women in positions of power. Sadly, the current women’s leadership in Pakistan is hardly representative of half the population. There are no women federal ministers, and only one woman minister of state. In Sindh, the PPP that brought us a woman prime minister has only two women cabinet members; while the party’s cabinet in Balochistan has only one woman minister. In KP, the PTI has no women in the cabinet. A woman chief minister leads Punjab, but her cabinet has only two women ministers, with Marriyum Aurangzeb holding six portfolios. As a pluralist federal democracy, at least on paper, Pakistan must move in line with Article 25 of the Constitution that empowers the government to make special provisions to protect women and children, apart from ensuring equal treatment for them. Women political prisoners, along with men, must be released; and women being half the population must be given half of the governing share. We owe this to every young girl in Pakistan. The writer is director of Bolo Bhi, an advocacy forum for digital rights. X: @UsamaKhilji Published in Dawn, August 24th, 2026

Unlearnt lessons of history. TODAY, the country’s hybrid government is fixated on altering Pakistan’s constitutionally mandated provincial structure and multiplying administrative units. To sell the idea, establishment apologists have rolled out some disingenuous arguments. They claim this will improve governance and miraculously solve the country’s problems overnight. A debate has been generated in the media about the pros and cons of administrative changes and breaking provinces into more units. Parliament has yet to discuss this. That is unsurprising. Deliberation is not this legislature’s strong suit. It has rushed through constitutional amendments in record time, once in the dead of night and without meaningful debate. Meanwhile, speculation is mounting that another constitutional amendment is being prepared to push through ‘administrative changes’. Absent from the establishment’s consideration of these sweeping changes are lessons from Pakistan’s history. Over the decades, the country’s rulers have experimented with parliamentary, presidential, semi-presidential, quasi-parliamentary systems, direct military rule, and more recently a hybrid model, which involves informal power-sharing between the military and civilians, with the former as dominant partner. Pakistan has tried them all. Yet each switch only contributed to political instability. The only system to command legitimacy and broad support is parliamentary democracy, despite the fact that parliamentary supremacy over the executive has never been realised. Linked to these experiments has been the status and rights of provinces in a federal system. As the provincial configuration and federating units largely coincided with the ethnic composition of people of each province, the need was always felt to make federalism a reality, not just a constitutional precept to ensure the people of all four provinces felt they were part of an inclusive and fair system. Pakistan’s troubled history offers a cautionary lesson against altering the provincial structure. But the federal structure and provincial rights have always been contested issues in Pakistan’s history. Contested on many counts. Smaller provinces have long resented Punjab’s political hegemony, sought greater powers and autonomy and felt the distribution of resources has been unfair. Unelected institutions have always preferred a centralised polity while military rule meant the country functioned as a virtual unitary state. Long periods of unrepresentative rule fuelled alienation among the smaller provinces by marginalising them, suppressing regional identities, concentrating power at the centre and weakening federalism. The creation of One Unit in the 1950s, which merged all the provinces of what was then West Pakistan into a single unit, was aimed at creating ‘parity’ with the more populous eastern wing of the country to undercut its numerical majority. This politically motivated project imposed a unitary system and all but destroyed the country’s federal character. It was justified by totally false and frivolous arguments. They included claims it would end “provincial prejudices”, reduce adm­i­nistrative expenses and help develop backward areas. The move had disastrous consequences. It fanned the flames of nationalist and regionalist sentiment in the smaller provinces of West Pak­istan and strengthened centrifugal forces across the country. It contributed to the sense of discrimination among the people of East Pakistan that, along with other factors, found expression in the Bengali nationalist movement and ultimately led to the break-up of Pakistan in 1971. The issue of provincial rights continued to be a source of tensions and contestation. The 1973 Constitution struck a delicate balance between the centre and provinces in a multiethnic state, assured provincial autonomy and enjoined reciprocal obligations between the federating units. Unfortunately, this was observed more in its breach than in its adherence. Opposition-run provincial governments were ousted in the 1970s by prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. This reinforced a political tradition that began in the early years after independence when provincial governments were summarily dismissed by the central government. This seriously undermined national unity. These and other actions widened interprovincial disparities, deepened alienation among smaller provinces and led to the insurgency in Balochistan in the 1970s. This intensified during the 2000s but their antecedents reached back to the 1950s. The insurgency continues today as a result of monumental mishandling of the province and Baloch sentiment by successive governments. Authoritarian measures also gave a fillip to Pakhtun nationalism, even though over time this waned with the increasing representation of KP in the country’s power elite and bure­aucracy. The troubled history of federalism and provincial tensions in Pakistan offers a cautionary lesson against altering the country’s four ethnically distinct provinces. Past attempts to do that or erode constitutionally guaranteed provincial rights only widened fault lines and created new ones. These efforts were never about better governance or a stronger administrative system. They were about control. They reflected the interests of a ruling elite seeking to entrench political dominance, with little regard for national unity and cohesion. The same logic applies to those in the current hybrid government pushing to create new provinces and fragment existing ones. This is about control, not reform. True ethnic minorities in some provinces, such as Seraiki speakers in southern Punjab, have long wanted their own province. Some political parties have actively supported this. But the challenge is how to square this with carving out a new unit that could undermine the delicate constitutional balance, spark controversy and encourage others to demand new provinces. The 18th Constitutional Amendment , backed by all parties in 2010, opened a new chapter in provincial empowerment. Over a dozen ministries were devolved from the federal level to the provinces. But this also raised capacity issues and whether provinces could handle the increased fiscal power and resources devolved to them. The fiscal aspect evoked the most criticism. Because with the 2009 National Finance Commission award, the substantial transfer of resources to the provinces left the federal government unable to meet its financial obligations. While this tussle over revenue needs to be resolved and provinces should mobilise their own resources, creating smaller provinces or rolling back the amendment is not the answer. In fact, the rationale for redrawing provincial boundaries remains opaque. This lack of clarity reinforces the impression that the motive is to increase control, not to improve governance. If we want real reform, it’s not by carving out new provinces. It’s by empowering local government. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN. Published in Dawn, August 24th, 2026

3 weeks on, nightly protests over Mir Raza’s murder continue in Karachi. • Family, friends and citizens gather on Sharea Faisal every night to demand justice • Vow to continue their demonstrations until those responsible for his death are arrested KARACHI: Family, friends, acquaintances and civil society members have been gathering on Sharea Faisal near Nursery every night for the past three weeks, blocking the key artery and vowing that they would not give up until justice is provided to slain Mir Raza Ali , whose body with a gunshot wound was found on July 29 at a desolate spot in Gulistan-i-Jauhar. More than 26 days after the murder, the identity of his killer(s) is yet to be known, compelling civil society to take to the streets on a daily basis. The Nursery bus stop has been turned into a focal point, where a large banner inscribed with ‘Justice for Mir Raza’ is displayed at the centre. The protesters include Raza’s family and friends, and dozens of men, women, their children and people of different age groups who have been demanding the arrest of Raza’s killers and exemplary punishment for them. On Saturday night, people turned out in large numbers and blocked both tracks of Sharea Faisal, staging a sit-in there until the wee hours of Sunday. During a visit to the protest site in the small hours of Sunday, protesters were seen using clapping as a collective expression of defiance and solidarity, blending it with their chants to create a wall of sound that carries far beyond the protest site. At times, the chanting, applause and calls for justice merge with the sound of drizzle and the movement of the night air, lending the gathering an atmosphere of persistence and resolve. A large number of participants raise their hands while chanting slogans and voicing their demands; some hold placards and banners bearing the words ‘Justice for Mir Raza’, making their presence felt, while others explain the protest’s background and history to those arriving for the first time. During the protest, one person can be seen addressing the gathering from the stage in memory of Raza, while another wipes away tears as emotions run high. Some protesters alternately climb onto water tankers placed by the police to block the roads and address the crowd from above, raising slogans against the police and the government. From time to time, slogans rise from the stage: ‘ Mir, hum sharminda hain, tere qatil zinda hain ’ (Mir, we are ashamed, your killers are still free) and ‘ Allah ka qanoon hai, khoon ka badla khoon hai’ (It is Allah’s law; blood must be avenged with blood). In other moments, speakers seek to keep Raza’s memory alive while impressing upon the crowd that his killing was not merely the loss of an individual but, in their view, an assault on the hopes and aspirations of Karachi’s young people. The stage reverberates with chants: ‘ Zinda hai Mir, zinda hai; bhaiyon ki shakal mein zinda hai, beton ki shakal mein zinda hai; zinda hai Mir, zinda hai ’ (Mir lives on, he lives on; he lives on in the face of brothers, he lives on in the face of sons; Mir lives on). At other times, the crowd raises the slogan: ‘Mir, tere khoon se inqilab aayega, raigan na jayega, inqilab aayega ’ (Mir, your blood will bring revolution; it will not go in vain; revolution will come). ‘We will not let Raza’s blood be in vain’ Dawn spoke to some of the participants who said that they would come daily to record their protest and would not give up hope until the killers were arrested. Alleging that the authorities were showing disregard for the grieving family, the protesters said, “The powerful think people would get tired of protesting in a few more days, but we [protesters] assure them that we will stand and protest for Raza, despite it taking months or even a year. We will not let his blood be in vain. We will bring his family justice.” On one side, dozens of men and women sit on rugs spread across the road, responding to slogans raised from the stage with enthusiasm and unwavering intensity. On the other, groups of youngsters spread across both tracks of Sharea Faisal, chanting at the top of their voices for the authorities’ resignation over what they describe as their failure to deliver justice. The presence of women, men and children gives the gathering the character of a broad-based public protest. Many had come with their families while others said they were taking time out of their daily routines to join the demonstration. Among the regular protesters is a woman known as “Apa”. She told Dawn that she did not know Raza or his family personally and had only met him once when she visited his eatery. “But when I came to know that he had been murdered in such a way, I could not tolerate it,” she said. She said she had children of her own and could understand what the family was going through. “This is not a jungle where we are living. It is a city. Even in a jungle there are laws,” she added. Apa said she would continue attending the protest and would be the last person to leave unless justice was provided. She said she remained hopeful that the truth would emerge and those responsible for Raza’s death would be arrested. For Raza’s friend Hassan Surya, the protest began before the family’s demonstration. When Raza went missing, he said, friends and family initially thought that he might have left home after becoming upset over “something personal”. They continued searching for him and when “we found out that he had been murdered in such a way, I started the protest”, he said. He said the family was busy with the investigation and other matters at the time. Hassan and some friends initially staged the protest at Charminar Chowrangi, Baha­durabad and later shifted it to Sharea Faisal, where it grew in size. Some of his close friends have since stopped coming regularly, he lamented, but he has continued to attend. Hassan said protesters had repeatedly become hopeful when the government appeared to take action, but their hopes were followed by frustration. “They keep creating diversions and excuses,” he said. “But we will not back down.” Two other protesters said that they had been attending the demonstration for around 15 days. They said they had joined because anyone murdered in such circumstances deserved justice. One of them said the protest had initially attracted fewer people but was gradually turning into a public movement as more citizens joined. He added that the government had yet to take any meaningful action on their demands. Published in Dawn, August 24th, 2026

Lahore traffic police going beyond the road for recovery of e-challan dues. LAHORE: Chief Traffic Officer (CTO) Syed Abdul Raheem Shirazi has sent recommendations to the higher authorities to link the recovery of pending digital traffic challans to the core services of computerised national identity cards (CNICs), passports, sale/purchase of vehicles and police services, a move being considered ‘most controversial in the history of the traffic police’. The proposal is said to be a blatant violation of the constitutional rights of citizens and the judgments of the Supreme Court. Through an official letter, the CTO has suggested to the Punjab DIG traffic police to make a move to stop the issuance of duplicate CNICs, renewal of passports, vehicle transfer (sale/purchase transactions) and certain police services to the citizens/defaulters at the police Khidmat centres across the city, an uncalled for proposal that has raised eyebrows among the police circles and legal fraternity. Citing the CTO’s recommendations as an attempt to infringe upon the constitutional rights of citizens for generating revenue or recovery of pending payments, a law firm is all set to challenge the ‘executive order of an individual officer’ in the Lahore High Court (LHC). Propose making CNIC, passport issuance, vehicles sale/purchase conditional to clearance of e-challan dues; legal expert terms the move illegal A spokesperson for the City Traffic Police confirmed to Dawn that CTO Shirazi had proposed a comprehensive mechanism for the recovery of pending payments on e-challans. He said the decision was made to tighten the net around e-challan defaulters by making police, CNIC and passport services conditional to the digital challan clearance. “A formal communication in this regard has been sent to the DIG Traffic Punjab and the Punjab Information Technology Department (PITB),” said the spokesperson while quoting the CTO’s letter. The CTO has proposed that, as in the case of e-challan default, the provision of certain services at Police Khidmat Markaz should also be linked to the clearance of outstanding digital challan dues. The spokesperson added that timely recovery of outstanding digital challans would also help expedite the disposal of cases pending before courts. “It would increase government revenue while reducing the administrative efforts and expenditure involved in the recovery process,” he added. A senior lawyer, Omais Younis, declared the proposal of the CTO Lahore childish and funny, saying that the law does not allow such exercises/practices as the SC has protected the rights of the citizens in many reported judgements. “The Supreme Court has held that even a court executing a money decree cannot block a CNIC where the governing law does not authorise that mode of execution,” the lawyer said and added that an unadjudicated or disputed traffic challan provided an even weaker legal basis for such a deprivation. “Article 10-A guarantees fair trial and due process in the determination of civil rights and obligations and criminal accusations. A digital challan begins as an allegation; it is not necessarily a final adjudication merely because it appears in a government database,” said Mr Younis. “Withholding a CNIC for a traffic fine is not a traffic-specific inconvenience,” said the lawyer, adding that it might disable large areas of a person’s legal, economic and social life and might adversely affect family members. “The same is the case with the issuance of the passport which is a legal document that allows the citizen for free and safe travel,” the lawyer added. Referring to a judgement of the Supreme Court given on Feb 18, 2026, Omais said Supreme Court of Pakistan declared that even an executing court cannot block a judgment-debtor’s Computerised National Identity Card (CNIC) to enforce a money decree or demand security, ruling the practice illegal and beyond the jurisdiction of civil courts. “The court held that section 51 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides recognised modes of execution but does not authorise CNIC blockage”, he said, quoting the SC verdict. He added the SC had also stressed that a CNIC is not a luxury or a mere statutory formality. “We are moving the court of law against the unlawful and unconstitutional proposal of the CTO for the sake of protecting the rights vested under the laws to citizens,” said Omais. Published in Dawn, August 24th, 2026

CDF Munir to visit Tehran on Monday, says Iranian foreign ministry. Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir will visit Tehran on Monday to continue efforts to bring peace ​and security to the region, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil ‌Baqaei said on Sunday, according to a statement by the ministry. He said CDF Munir would lead an official delegation and the “visit aims to strengthen bilateral cooperation between Iran and Pakistan and to continue Pakistan’s good offices in support of peace and security in the region”. During the visit, CDF Munir would meet and hold talks with senior officials Iran, Baqaei added. The visit comes amid heightened tensions as ‌Iran threatens ⁠a military response to US plans for sanctions that could further put a strain on the Islamic republic’s ailing economy. It will coincide with a Monday announcement on details related to the planned sanctions, which ​US officials have ​said would be “ the ⁠toughest sanctions in history ” on Iran. Trump had warned of economic consequences against any country that provided “any type ​of lifeline to Iran” as he seeks to isolate ​the ⁠Islamic republic. Oil shipments are at a virtual standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran threatening to strike any unauthorised oil tankers that ⁠try to ​transit the vital waterway, and Iran’s ​economy is already under immense pressure from sanctions. Pakistan’s mediation Pakistan has been leading mediation efforts between the two sides in the ongoing war, which began with US and ​Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Less than two months after the beginning of the war, Pakistan brokered a ceasefire between the two sides on April 8 and Islamabad hosted direct talks between US and Iran on April 11 and 12. The mediation efforts also led to the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on June 17 between the US and Iran in Geneva. The MoU set a framework to move towards a permanent end to the war. While hostilities have renewed between the two sides since, Pakistan remains engaged in mediation efforts, with CDF Munir and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi having made multiple visits to Iran in recent months.

Pakistan to host South Asian Games in April next year. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan will host the South Asian Games from April 3 to 11 next year, 23 years after it last staged the regional sports gala in Islamabad in 2004. The decision was taken at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the South Asia Olympic Council held here on Sunday, with Pakistan Olympic Association (POA) president Arif Saeed, who is also president of the South Asian Olympic Committee, in the chair. The meeting reviewed preparations for the Games and approved three host cities — Islamabad, Lahore and Peshawar. Representatives from Bangladesh, Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka attended the meeting in person, while India participated through video link. All the representatives endorsed the proposed dates, according to sources. A visiting delegation is scheduled to inspect proposed sporting venues in Islamabad on Monday. The Games will feature 28 sports and 346 medal events, with more than 3,200 athletes expected to participate across the three host cities. A large number of technical officials will also be part of the event, with Pakistan preparing to host around 4,000 athletes and other foreign visitors. During Sunday’s meeting, representatives of the participating countries reviewed preparations and measures being taken by Pakistan to host the regional event. The federal government has already given the go-ahead to the POA and other stakeholders to hold the Games and announced that the required funds would be released. Pakistan was originally scheduled to host the Games in 2021, but the event was subsequently postponed for various reasons. Preparations are now said to be in their final stages. The visiting delegation also visited the Taxila Museum and other historical sites on Sunday. Sources said the Capital Development Authority (CDA), on the direction of the federal government, had started preparations to provide accommodation and other facilities to foreign visitors arriving in Islamabad next year for the South Asian Games and other international events, including the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) conference. “The federal government has been taking every possible step to make the three international events next year in Islamabad highly successful — the South Asian Games, SCO conference and a meeting of the OIC,” a senior government official told Dawn . He said the POA, Foreign Office and federal government were monitoring preparations to ensure that the Games were hosted successfully. “Everyone is on board and working as a team for these Games,” he said. Asked about India’s participation, the official said its representative had joined Sunday’s meeting through video link and endorsed the dates, which, according to him, indicated that India intended to participate. However, another source cautioned that India’s participation could not yet be confirmed. “India has been mixing politics with sports and has avoided visiting Pakistan. Even recently, it did not participate in a volleyball event,” the source said. Published in Dawn, August 24th, 2026

Amnesty International says police in India used excessive force during youth-led protests. Indian police used excessive force, including electric shock devices and pellet guns, against youth-led protests that forced the education minister to resign last month, Amnesty International said on Monday. A report from the rights group clashes with the police account that force was used only after protesters turned violent, and comes after India’s Supreme Court set up a panel on Thursday to investigate violence by both police and demonstrators. Demonstrations in the capital New Delhi, triggered by the leak of the national medical entrance test, turned violent on July 20 when thousands of protesters attempted to march towards parliament. Amnesty said witness testimony and visual evidence it had verified confirmed the use of “pellet-firing shotguns, tear gas launchers, grenades, batons and electric shock devices against protesters” in Delhi and the eastern state of Bihar. Amnesty said it had also verified two instances of a police officer “unlawfully using lethal force against a crowd” in Bihar’s Siwan district. No one was killed. “The weapons were deployed in a manner that breached international law and standards and domestic policing guidelines,” it added. Amnesty said that there were “isolated incidents of protesters throwing stones”, but that the “heavy-handed response was state-sanctioned violence masked as crowd control”. Delhi Police said in a Supreme Court hearing last week they had used force only after protesters “resorted to violence”. They said anti-social elements “masquerading as aggrieved students” caused “grievous injuries” to security forces. On Friday, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi staged a sit-in outside a Delhi police station with a 19-year-old protester who said he was injured by pellets during the July 20 demonstration. Gandhi demanded a police investigation into the shooting, and officers later registered a case over the complaint. Led by the online Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the protests broadened from anger over exam irregularities into a wider movement over unemployment, opportunities for young people and what critics describe as Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s increasingly authoritarian rule. The protests proved to be the biggest challenge that Modi has faced after winning a third term in 2024.

Amin Mughal taught Pakistan’s Left and media to disagree without falling apart. Amin Mughal, who died in London on August 12, 2026, spent a lifetime translating between Pakistan’s revolutionaries, dissidents and journalists so their fractured Left could at least understand itself. In 1981, the state arrested three editors at once: Mazhar Ali Khan, I.A. Rehman and Amin Mughal, all picked up in the same sweep. The weekly they ran, Viewpoint , did not miss an issue. Zafar Iqbal Mirza, ZIM to everyone who knew him, held the paper together from the inside while the men who built it sat in cells. That is the kind of loyalty this story is about, and it says more about who Amin Mughal was than any list of his credentials could. Much has already been written about the shape of his life since his death : the teaching, the imprisonment, the journalism, the years abroad. None of it explains what made him necessary. The photograph This is a photograph, taken years ago, of six men. In front: ZIM, Shafqat Tanvir Mirza, Dada Ameer Hyder and I.A. Rehman. Behind them: Major Ishaq Muhammad, remembered for the Rawalpindi Conspiracy Case, and Amin Mughal. Front row, from left: Zafar Iqbal Mirza (ZIM), Shafqat Tanvir Mirza, Dada Ameer Hyder and I.A. Rehman. Second row: Major Ishaq Muhammad and Professor Amin Mughal. Photo: Dr Ikram Ul Haq None of them sought celebrity, which is presumably why the state never bothered to give them any. Together they made up a moral republic Pakistan has never formally admitted existed. The photograph works not because these six men agreed on everything. They didn’t. It works because it captures how different a resistance can look from the inside: the organiser, the dissident soldier, the journalist, the editor, the human rights defender, the guardian of a language nobody in power wanted spoken. Mughal stands in the second row, not the centre, though he belonged at the centre of the intellectual relationships represented in the photo. That was the pattern of his life. He showed up, he listened, he stayed connected to everyone, and he never once needed to be the main character. What he actually did Mughal’s contribution wasn’t a body of work. It was a set of connections that would not otherwise have existed. He linked the organised Left of Dada Ameer Hyder and Major Ishaq to the democratic journalism of ZIM and I.A. Rehman, to the cultural resistance of Shafqat Tanvir Mirza, and eventually to younger reporters like myself, who came up in journalism without fully grasping what had been handed to them. I worked under him at Viewpoint between 1979 and 1984, in a cramped office at 4-Lawrence Road, Lahore, that functioned as my real education. Mazhar Ali Khan had assembled people who treated journalism as an ethical obligation rather than a career strategy, and Mughal fit that room completely. He never separated editing from teaching, or political analysis from literature, or disagreement from affection. Most people manage one of those. He ran all four at once. The coal-boy who organised the world Dada Ameer Hyder started as a coal-boy on a ship, which is not the kind of biographical detail you can invent. By the time most Pakistanis had learned the word “globalisation,” he had already lived it: labour, empire and racial hierarchy, encountered directly, on the ground, from Bombay and Moscow to New York, Shanghai and Buenos Aires. He organised workers across borders before international solidarity became a phrase people used at funded conferences. The author met him at Viewpoint . He carried none of the theatre you’d expect from a man with that resume. His authority came from what he’d survived, not from what he claimed. Official histories mostly left him out, for a simple reason: independence movements can absorb elite leaders. A worker who kept asking what independence had actually delivered to other workers is a harder problem, and states tend to solve hard problems by ignoring them. The soldier who wouldn’t let it go Major Ishaq was a soldier who thought past the limits of the uniform, which got him implicated in the Rawalpindi Conspiracy Case and imprisoned more than once. After Hasan Nasir died in custody, Ishaq kept pushing on the question of how, at a moment when silence would have cost him far less. Later, he organised peasants and workers, treating revolution as slow, unglamorous construction rather than slogan. Even paralysis didn’t stop him. His life refused the tidy categories people like to sort dissidents into: soldier or critic, patriot or traitor. He was, inconveniently, both halves of each pair. The language they tried to bury Shafqat Tanvir Mirza fought with a different weapon: language itself. As a journalist, trade unionist, historian and scholar, he understood that Punjabi’s marginalisation wasn’t an accident of literary fashion. It was a people being cut off from their own memory, by design. His scholarship on Punjabi literature and the Sufi poets gave institutional weight back to a language spoken by millions and taken seriously by almost no one in power. It cost him imprisonment and professional setbacks. It never cost him his willingness to sit down and actually talk to people who disagreed with him. The marathon I.A. Rehman took those same commitments and built an institution around defending human rights. His life made an argument most people never manage to prove: that fighting injustice for decades doesn’t have to curdle into bitterness. He spoke softly, listened, and did not move. He went to prison twice for telling the truth and never once framed it as sacrifice, because for him it was simply the price of meaning what he said. His own description of the work has outlasted him: the struggle for human rights, he said, is a marathon, not a sprint. In a country now addicted to instant outrage and equally instant despair, that line does more work than most policy papers. The translator So what set Mughal apart from four people this formidable? He was the one who could move between their worlds without flattening any of them. From Dada Ameer Hyder and Major Ishaq, he took the demand for structural change. From Shafqat Tanvir Mirza, the idea that culture and liberation are the same fight. From ZIM, professional integrity. From I.A. Rehman, the insistence on everyone’s dignity, no exceptions. He absorbed all of it without turning any single strand into dogma, which is a harder trick than it sounds. He could dismantle a bad argument without touching the dignity of the person making it, and younger colleagues learned more from watching him do that than from anything he assigned them to read. Progressive politics without intellectual honesty curdles into just another orthodoxy. Journalism without moral purpose is merchandise. Scholarship without human sympathy is vanity. He never had to say this out loud. He just modelled it, repeatedly, until it stuck. What’s left The photograph is also a record of a sociology that doesn’t really exist anymore: people meeting in newspaper offices, union halls, study circles, cramped homes and cheap cafés, with no research grants and no communications department, running entirely on conversation, print and organising. They disagreed constantly. Disagreement never required excommunication, and friendship never required conformity. Pakistan now has more universities, television channels, and policy shops than the country in that photograph could have imagined. It has fewer rooms where knowledge, courage and humility actually meet in the same place. Dissent has become something you measure in visibility. Causes are managed like careers. The six men in that photograph belonged to a harder tradition, one where ideas were tested by what you were willing to lose for them. Mughal’s death stings in a specific way: he was one of the last living bridges to that tradition. He connected generations without asking for discipleship. He kept memory alive without becoming its warden. His politics were never against faith or culture. They were against every structure built to humiliate people. The easy response to a photograph like this is nostalgia, which lets the living off the hook while it honours the dead. The harder question is what happened to the republic these six men were silently building, and whether anything is being built to replace it. Their Pakistan never fully arrived. It also wasn’t imaginary. It existed anywhere truth was spoken without hedging, language was rescued, workers got organised, prisoners were defended, censorship was resisted, and young people were treated like they mattered. All six men in that photograph are gone now. History will not fill the space they left on its own.

Polls underway for 7 reserved seats in AJK Legislative Assembly today. Elections on seven reserved seats in the Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) Legislative Assembly are currently underway. Polling began after 10am and will continue until 1pm. Under Article 22(1) of the AJK Constitution, the Legislative Assembly consists of 53 members, including 45 members elected directly through adult franchise and eight members chosen by directly elected representatives. The reserved seats include five seats for women and one each for Ulema-i-Din or Mashaikh well-versed in the teachings of Islam, Jammu and Kashmir State subjects residing abroad, and technocrats and other professionals. PML-N’s Chaudhry Abdul Rehman Arain was the only candidate to have submitted his nomination papers for the seat reserved for state subjects residing abroad. He was consequently declared elected unopposed. Elections to seven of the 45 directly elected seats — five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district — could not be held due to the law and order situation in the region. As a result, the 38 members elected so far, representing 84.4 per cent of the directly elected membership, will participate in the reserved seat elections. Six candidates will contest five seats reserved for women, according to the final list issued by the Election Commission on Sunday. The candidates in the fray are PML-N’s Riffat Abid, Sehrish Qamar, Maryam Idrees and Maryam Zaman, also known as Maryam Kashmiri, and PPP’s Farzana Yaqoob and Zobia Khurshid Raja. For the seat reserved for Ulema and Mashaikh, PPP’s Hafiz Tariq Mahmood will face PML-N’s Mohammad Mazhar Saeed. Similarly, PML-N’s Barrister Syed Iftikhar Gillani and PPP’s Sahibzada Zulfiqar Ali will contest the seat reserved for technocrats and professionals. As the inaugural session of the incoming Legislative Assembly has already been summoned for 2pm on Monday, shortly after the announcement of the results, all newly elected members will take an oath at the hands of outgoing Speaker Chaudhry Latif Akbar, who failed to retain his seat in the elections. AJK polls The elections in the region, originally scheduled for July 27, were divided into phases over security concerns amid unrest in the region. The first phase was held on July 27, the second on Aug 2 and the third on Aug 10. The third phase was originally meant to cover all of Poonch Division, which comprises 11 constituencies, including three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district. However, the AJK Election Commission announced that polling would only go ahead as scheduled in Bagh and Haveli because of concerns over the law and order situation. So far, in the direct elections to 38 constituencies, the PML-N has secured 25 seats while the PPP won 12. The lone MLA-elect of the Awami Dast-o-Bazu party has also joined hands with the PML-N . The PPP has alleged widespread rigging in the polls, with the party also ramping up its criticism of the ruling PML-N in recent days. Last week, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said that a genuine alliance with the PML-N was not possible until their grievances regarding the AJK polls were addressed as he established formal contact with the PTI and offered to cooperate with the party in Parliament. Speaking to the media, the PPP chairman alleged that the AJK election process had been made controversial for political interests. He alleged that the federal government’s political and administrative machinery had remained active in AJK throughout the six-phase election process, raising serious questions over its transparency. The PPP, he said, had raised its objections before the Election Commission, parliament and other constitutional forums, but the PML-N had failed to address its concerns or engage in meaningful dialogue after the polls. Moreover, he said the commitments and political understandings reached with the PML-N before the prime minister’s election had not been honoured. The PPP had cooperated in the wider national interest, he said, but there could be no genuine alliance with the PML-N unless the party’s concerns over the AJK elections were addressed and political commitments fulfilled. He pointed out that the government needed PPP’s votes for several important laws, constitutional amendments and difficult bills. He said legislation could not be forced through on the basis of a majority or through coercion. The discord between the PPP and PML-N was also apparent in the National Assembly on Aug 18, when the former managed to compel the government to virtually suspend the heavy legislative agenda for the day, which included 21 bills. On Aug 20, when the lower house of Parliament passed two bills pertaining to the military and nuclear command structure, the PPP also objected to the manner in which the legislation was presented. While the party ultimately voted in favour of the bills, Bilawal lashed out at the government for not taking ruling allies on board.

Info ministry says video of defence minister comparing Pakistan with India is fake. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting on Monday said that a video of Defence Minister Khawaja Asif comparing Pakistan’s progress with India’s was “fake”, adding that the PML-N leader had not made any such statement. The ministry shared the purported clip of the minister on its X account. The nearly minute-long video appeared to show a clip from a press conference by the minister on a major news channel. In the purported video, the minister called on citizens to review the country’s situation. He went on to say that Pakistan and India had gained independence at the same time, yet the difference in progress between the two was evident. The purported clip showed Asif saying that Balochistan had “slipped from our hands”, the people in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa were facing difficulties and residents of Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) had taken to the streets for their rights. On the other hand, look at India, Asif said in the alleged video, pointing to the country’s progress in technology, infrastructure and the economy. “We have to ask ourselves whether we are a true democracy. Instead of blaming others, we should question our government and policies,” Asif said in the purported clip. The clip, which was circulating on social media, was also picked up by Indian media, with News18 publishing an article on the alleged statement by Asif. Sharing the clip on X, the information ministry said on Monday: “This news is FAKE and the voice in the video is AI-generated. “Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has not given any such statement. Please verify news from official sources before sharing,” it said. The same statement was also shared by the information ministry’s fact-checking account on X.

Recovered from him were a .45-caliber pistol, five magazines, 49 rounds of live ammunition, and a black belt bag. Noe was brought to the Station Investigation and Detection Management Section for further investigation and the filing of complaints for alleged usurpation of authority and violation of Republic Act No. 10591, or the Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act.

'Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie': The best kind of clean, positive fun. The latest screen outing of the ever-lovable pups, "Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie," is a cheerful, exciting adventure that gives us just the kind of clean, positive fun kids nowadays need to see. The movie follows Ryder and his pups as they find themselves stranded on a mysterious island where, somehow, Dinosaurs still roam. On the island they meet Rex, a disabled Bernese Mountain Dog who relies on a sort of high-tech wheelchair to make up for his hind legs that aren’t working properly. Rex has appeared in the show as well, and while older folks will undoubtedly try to figure out a timeline when exactly the movie takes place in the continuity of the show, most kids will simply take things as they are and lean into the fun of it. No one bothers to figure out how Ryder can afford all the things he conjures up for his canine companions (His last name is probably STARK). There are talking pups and living breathing dinosaurs, so of course the only thing to do is enjoy it. The Pups have never looked better, sporting high-end movie-level visuals, as well as an all new set of dinosaur-themed vehicles and outfits. The parents out there who grew up in the era of "GI Joe" and "Transformers" know precisely what this means. It's time for a line-wide refresh, ushering a brand new set of toys and merchandise to sell to screaming kids and defenseless moms and dads. But far from being cynical about it, even as a parent who could potentially shell out money once the movie hits, I don’t mind it all that much. I enjoyed the movie maybe as much as my eight-year old, exactly because it reminds me so much of the shows I enjoyed as a kid. There’s no nostalgia, but it does capture the vibe of adventure and wonder that seem to be lacking in a social-media-dominated world. And the merch, well, anything (within a reasonable price range) that encourages imaginative play is something to be welcomed. Of course a Paw Patrol adventure would not be complete without the complication of Mayor Humdinger and his Catastrophe Crew. Fresh out of jail, Mayor Humdinger reverts back to his greedy self and hatches a plan to strip the island of it’s rare diamonds, to catastrophic results. Just as in the previous movies, one pup out of the six takes center stage, and this time it’s Marshall. The clumsy dalmatian does a bit of maturing in this film, just as Chase and Sky did in their previous theatrical outings. The themes of friendship, loyalty and perseverance are woven heavily into the story, but are never dolled out with a heavy hand. There’s a lot of heart underneath all the adventure and thrills, which is just the way it is supposed to be. With this new Dinosaur movie, Paw Patrol remains 100% parent-approved, at least by this child of the 80’s.

‘Spider-Man’ tops box office in fourth weekend; ‘The Odyssey’ becomes Nolan’s highest-grossing film. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” fought off a slew of newcomers, including a comedy, a horror franchise, a Jason Statham action movie and a family pic, to maintain its first-place spot at the box office in its fourth weekend in theaters. “The Odyssey” also became Christopher Nolan’s highest grossing movie ever, both domestically and internationally. For the year, “The Odyssey” is second only to “Spider-Man,” which added $39 million from 4,006 theaters in the U.S. and Canada, according to studio estimates Sunday. “Spider-Man,” which has now made over $854.9 million in North America, will soon surpass “Avengers: Endgame” to become the second highest-grossing domestic release of all time. The record holder is currently “Star Wars: The Force Awakens” ($936.7 million). Sony also had the second biggest movie of the weekend with “Insidious: Out of the Further.” The sixth movie in the franchise, produced by Blumhouse Atomic Monster, made $25.3 million from 3,303 theaters. Internationally, it made $35 million. Its $18 million production budget makes it the most expensive movie of the series. Third place went to “The Odyssey,” which earlier this week became the highest grossing R-rated movie of all time, surpassing “Deadpool & Wolverine.” It added $19.5 million in its sixth weekend in North American theaters, where it continues to play in over 3,000 locations, bringing its domestic total to just under $539.1 million. That pushes it past the $534.9 million from “The Dark Knight” — a previous high-water mark for Nolan — not accounting for inflation. Internationally, it added $68 million, driven largely by China and Korea, which brings its worldwide total to $1.4 billion. The other big newcomers landed further down the charts. “Mutiny,” starring Statham as a man wrongly accused of murdering his billionaire boss, opened in sixth place with $7.5 million from 2,703 locations. The Lionsgate release (an acquisition) was intended to be a theatrical only release, but a few days before it opened it was accidentally available for free on Prime Video for a few hours before the mistake was remedied. The glitch might have impacted its opening weekend earnings, but the film also had some fairly bad reviews working against it. Even more poorly reviewed was “Spa Weekend,” a girl’s trip comedy from the men behind “The Hangover” and “Bad Moms,” starring Isla Fisher, Leslie Mann, Anna Faris and Michelle Buteau. It made an estimated $3.1 million in 2,009 locations. Women accounted for some 84% of opening weekend ticket buyers, according to PostTrak. The 25th anniversary re-release of “The Fast and the Furious” made slightly more. “The Magic Faraway Tree,” starring Andrew Garfield, opened outside of the top 10 with $1.4 million from 1,611 screens. The young Anthony Bourdain movie “Tony” continues to do quite well, however, earning $5 million from 1,652 screens. The summer season, which runs through Labor Day, has now generated an estimated $4.4 billion in ticket sales in North America, putting it among the top four highest grossing summers ever. “We’re in the home stretch of what I think will go down in box office history as maybe one of the most key and pivotal summer movie seasons ever,” said Paul Dergarabedian, the head of marketplace trends for Rentrak. “I don’t know how you can replicate this summer. Studios will try.” Michael O’Leary, the president and CEO of the movie theater trade organization Cinema United, noted the wide variety of movies in the marketplace that have helped contribute to a big summer. Part of that, he told The Associated Press, was that the industry pipeline is finally bouncing back from the effects of the Hollywood strikes in 2023. “The thing that I’m most excited about, frankly, is just the enthusiasm of moviegoers,” O’Leary said. “You feel it when you go to the theater. There’s an energy about being in the theater that hasn’t been there in the recent past.” The year overall has also surpassed $7 billion, which is up about 20.4% from 2025, but about 7.1% behind 2019. Top 10 movies by domestic box office With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak: 1. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” $39 million. 2. “Insidious: Out of the Further,” $25.3 million. 3. “The Odyssey,” $19.5 million. 4. “Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie,” $9.1 million. 5. “The End of Oak Street,” $9 million. 6. “Mutiny,” $7.5 million. 7. “Tony,” $5 million. 8. “The Fast and the Furious” (25th anniversary re-release), $3.1 million. 9. “Spa Weekend,” $3.1 million. 10. “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” $1.9 million. LINDSEY BAHR

Greenstrum partners with Huawei to launch ultra-fast commercial EV charger. Greenstrum is expanding its commercial footprint in the electric vehicle (EV) infrastructure market, offering white-label charging networks and battery storage systems directly to corporate fleets, property developers, and automotive manufacturers in the Philippines. In a statement, Greenstrum said the enterprise expansion aims to capitalize on rising demand for private EV charging facilities as companies attempt to electrify commercial fleets and commercial real estate assets. Under its enterprise model, Greenstrum handles the engineering, procurement, and construction of charging networks while allowing corporate clients to retain complete ownership and operational branding over the assets. A central element of the expansion relies on hardware and battery integration through global technology provider Huawei. Greenstrum deploys Huawei’s FusionCharge hardware, which ranges from seven-kilowatt direct current chargers to high-capacity 480-kilowatt fast chargers capable of replenishing compatible EV batteries within 10 to 15 minutes. To address grid constraints that often accompany high-output charging installations, Greenstrum is integrating Huawei’s LUNA2000 Smart Energy Storage Systems (BESS). The battery units act as buffer systems, capturing power during off-peak periods and discharging energy during high-demand sessions. This approach allows enterprise operators to deploy fast-charging stations without requiring costly utility grid upgrades or incurring severe peak-demand electricity charges. “Businesses have different goals in building their own EV infrastructure, whether it’s to operate their own fleets or to set up their own EV charging business," said Carl Decleodt, Chief Operations Officer at Greenstrum.” “Greenstrum can provide tailor-fit solutions to support this need through expert installation services, backed by superior equipment for both EV charging as well as battery technology, and a proven record of safety and service excellence,” it added. The enterprise move builds on Greenstrum’s experience as an installation partner for ACMobility's nationwide charging network. All installations are certified by professional electrical engineers in compliance with the Philippine Electrical Code, and commercial setups feature solar-ready wiring alongside integration into the Evro mobile application for user billing and station locator services. Through this push, Greenstrum joins a growing competitive race among regional infrastructure firms seeking to establish turn-key commercial charging networks across Southeast Asia as corporate vehicle fleet electrification gains momentum.

Kim Soo-hyun makes first public appearance through TV event in Indonesia. Actor Kim Soo-hyun made his first public appearance after more than a year in an event in Indonesia. The “Queen of Tears” star was a special guest on Indonesian TV network RCTI’s 37th anniversary event "Mahakarya RCTI 37" on Aug. 23. Wearing a white suit, Kim Soo-hyun greeted those present with a smile saying, “Thank you for inviting me to such a meaningful event." He also sang “Dreaming,” an original soundtrack from the 2011 Korean drama “Dream High” which he starred in. “Thank you Kim Soo-Hyun for coming to MAHAKRYA RCTI 37! Such a great moment,” RCTI posted on Instagram along with a video of Kim Soo-hyun. RCTI reported that hundreds of fans welcomed Kim Soo-hyun when he arrived at the MNC Studios in Kebon Jeruk, West Jakarta. He was welcomed by MNC Group Co-CEO Angela Tanoesoedibjo and RCTI President Director Valencia Tanoesoedibjo. “Mahakarya RCTI 37” featured performances, including from Indonesia’s top soap opera stars. One of the evening's treats was the wedding celebration between Sena and Davina from the Indonesian soap opera "Terikat Janji." The RCTI event was Kim Soo-hyun’s first public appearance in more than a year after getting embroiled in a controversy surrounding the late actress Kim Sae-ron. He has since been cleared by the police on allegations that he dated Kim Sae-ron when she was a minor. His main accuser, YouTuber Kim Se-ui of the channel HoverLab previous, was arrested for defamation.

P375K kush seized in Parañaque buy-bust; 2 arrested. Two men were arrested after police seized around 250 grams of high-grade marijuana or “kush” valued at P375,000 during a buy-bust operation in Parañaque City early Sunday morning, Aug. 23. The suspects, both 24, were identified as Paul, a resident of Barangay Moonwalk, and Mikko, of Barangay San Isidro. Police said operatives of the Station Drug Enforcement Unit (SDEU) of the Parañaque City Police Station conducted the operation at around 3:20 a.m. at a residence on Daang Batang Street in Barangay Moonwalk. Police said an undercover officer successfully purchased suspected kush from the suspects before the arresting team moved in. The operation resulted in the recovery of several sachets and plastic bags containing suspected high-grade marijuana weighing approximately 250 grams valued at P375,000. Police also recovered the P1,000 marked money used in the transaction, a smartphone, and an eco bag allegedly used to carry the suspected illegal drugs. Authorities are preparing charges against Paul for violation of Section 5 (sale) and Section 11 (possession) of Article II of Republic Act No. 9165, or the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002. Mikko, meanwhile, is facing a complaint for alleged violation of Section 5 of RA 9165. They were both detained at the police custodial facility after their arrest.
